cases.sector_theme: GPU-accelerated computing / datacenter-AI (deep learning) re-rating, pre-"AI stock" era
cases.run_window: Stock roughly tripled through calendar 2016 (closed 2015 near $32.96, unadjusted); the decisive re-rating print was the Q3 FY2017 earnings release on 2016-11-10 (record $2.00B quarterly revenue, +54% YoY), after which the multi-year 2016-2018 AI/datacenter re-rating accelerated. Market-cap trackers put NVDA at roughly $12-15B in mid/late 2015 and ~$37B by Nov 2016 (verified SEC non-affiliate-float figures corroborate the low end; the year-over-year multiple is directionally consistent across sources but I could not verify the exact monthly cap series myself).
cases.price_move: Non-affiliate market value of NVDA common stock was $9.38B as of 2014-07-25 (FY2015 10-K) and $9.92B as of 2015-07-24 (FY2016 10-K) — both figures I opened directly on SEC EDGAR. Third-party trackers (not independently verified by me beyond the search snippet) put total market cap near $12-15B through 2015 rising to ~$37B by November 2016, i.e., roughly a 2.5-3x move concentrated in 2016, continuing further into 2017-2018.

signals.name: SEC filings already used the words 'deep learning' and 'artificial intelligence' to describe Tesla GPUs 18-20 months before the run took off
signals.evidence: NVIDIA's FY2015 10-K (filed 2015-03-06, fiscal year ended Jan 25 2015) markets the Tesla brand for 'researchers, deep learning and big-data analysts' and, in the automotive risk discussion, states cars 'will use the tools of deep learning to sense their environment, ultimately driving themselves.' This is roughly 20 months before the 2016-11-10 earnings print that marked the visible re-rating. Non-affiliate market value at the time was only $9.38B (as of 2014-07-25), i.e. the company was still small-cap when it was already narrating this bet in a mandatory filing, not just in marketing copy.
signals.free_source: SEC EDGAR full-text search (10-K filings, free)

signals.name: Cloud-provider 'large project wins' called out in an SEC-filed CFO commentary, ~18 months before the run
signals.evidence: Q1 FY2016 CFO Commentary (period ended 2015-04-26, filed as an 8-K exhibit): 'Tesla GPUs for accelerated computing increased strongly, driven by large project wins with cloud service providers,' and management named 'deep learning, self-driving cars, and gaming' as the company's stated growth initiatives -- 18 months before the Nov-2016 print. No customer names given at this point (that came later), so this is a directional signal, not yet a hard anchor-customer confirmation.
signals.free_source: SEC EDGAR (8-K exhibits / CFO commentary, free)

signals.name: CEO publicly reframes the company around four new growth vectors, ~9 months before the run's inflection print
signals.evidence: Q4/FY2016 earnings release (issued 2016-02-17): CEO Jen-Hsun Huang stated 'NVIDIA is at the center of four exciting growth opportunities - PC gaming, VR, deep learning, and self-driving cars' and cited 'sharply growing customer engagements in deep learning' across life sciences, financial services and IoT. This reframed a legacy gaming-GPU company as a multi-market AI platform company in an earnings release almost a year before the market visibly re-rated it.
signals.free_source: Company IR press releases (free) / SEC 8-K exhibits

signals.name: Named hyperscaler and cloud customers (Facebook ML, Alibaba AliCloud HPC) disclosed in the FY2016 10-K, ~8 months before the inflection print
signals.evidence: FY2016 10-K (fiscal year ended 2016-01-31): 'Tesla GPUs and our cuDNN software have been broadly adopted for deep learning, a new computing method for enabling artificial intelligence.' It further discloses that 'Facebook [is] using the NVIDIA Tesla accelerated computing platform for machine learning applications' and that Alibaba's AliCloud is working with NVIDIA to build 'China's first GPU-accelerated, cloud-based, high performance computing platform.' Named hyperscaler customers in a 10-K are a stronger, more falsifiable signal than generic 'cloud service providers' language.
signals.free_source: SEC EDGAR (10-K filings, free)

signals.name: Revenue growth actually accelerated sharply the quarter the market re-rated the stock (the confirming, not leading, signal)
signals.evidence: Q3 FY2017 earnings release (issued 2016-11-10): record quarterly revenue of $2.00B, up 54% year-over-year, with CEO stating 'Our GPU deep learning platform runs every AI framework, and is available in cloud services from Amazon, IBM, Microsoft and Alibaba, and in servers from every OEM.' This print is widely reported (though I did not independently verify the exact one-day stock move) as the moment the market decisively re-rated NVDA -- i.e. this is the confirmation event, not a leading indicator; the signals above (2015-early 2016) were the pieces an analyst could have had before this print.
signals.free_source: Company IR press releases (free) / SEC 8-K exhibits

signals.name: NVIDIA remained solidly GAAP-profitable throughout the pre-run window -- unlike the framing in the user's question about today's unprofitable 'bumper' candidates
signals.evidence: FY2016 (fiscal year ended 2016-01-31) GAAP net income was $614 million on $5.01B revenue (down 3% YoY due to a one-time $131M restructuring charge; non-GAAP net income grew 16% YoY to $929M). This is a structural point: the NVDA case is a profitable, self-funding company narrating a new market inside its existing profitable core business -- a materially different setup from an early-stage, cash-burning company (e.g. quantum-computing names) betting on a market that doesn't exist yet. Fundamentals-alone analysis would have flagged NVDA as 'fine but not obviously re-rate-worthy'; it would not have flagged an unprofitable pre-revenue name at all, which is the gap the user is trying to close.
signals.free_source: Company IR press releases / SEC EDGAR 10-K (free)

signals.name: A same-story competitor (Intel/Nervana + Movidius) chased the identical 'AI datacenter chip' narrative in the same window and it did not translate into a comparable re-rating
signals.evidence: Fortune (2016-08-09): Intel acquired AI-chip startup Nervana Systems, with Intel VP Jason Waxman framing AI as 'the next big wave' and touting Nervana's interconnect speed as 5-10x faster than 'traditional chips' -- explicitly positioned to 'challenge Nvidia's graphics processing dominance in machine learning.' Intel followed with the Movidius computer-vision-chip acquisition weeks later (Sept 2016). Both efforts used the same public narrative NVDA was using (deep learning, datacenter AI, cloud demand) at the same time, from a much larger, well-capitalized incumbent -- yet Intel's stock did not re-rate the way NVDA's did, and the Nervana chip line itself was later discontinued in favor of Habana Labs' Gaudi/Goya. This is the clearest same-era false positive: identical narrative, different market maker (CUDA software ecosystem lock-in vs. a hardware-only pitch), different outcome.
signals.free_source: Company press releases / trade press (free), SEC 8-K/10-K for Intel's own disclosures

cases.what_fundamentals_alone_missed: Fundamentals in 2014-2015 said "profitable, mid-single-digit revenue growth, gaming-cyclical GPU company" -- true, unremarkable, and would not by itself have flagged a multi-bagger. What fundamentals alone could not price in: (1) a *platform/ecosystem* moat (CUDA + cuDNN software stack) that determined which hardware vendor captured the coming deep-learning capex wave -- this is not a line item on an income statement, it shows up only in developer-adoption and framework-support signals; (2) the fact that the addressable market itself (GPU-accelerated deep learning training) barely existed as a reporting category yet -- NVIDIA was not yet breaking out "Datacenter" as its own segment with hard numbers in FY2015-early FY2016, so segment-level financial statements lagged the qualitative language in the same filings; (3) which specific named hyperscaler customers (Facebook, Baidu, Alibaba) were already running production/research workloads on the hardware, since that determines whether the narrative converts to backlog; (4) that a nominally identical narrative pursued by a much larger competitor (Intel/Nervana) would fail to re-rate the incumbent, meaning the "AI datacenter" theme alone was not sufficient -- ecosystem lock-in was the differentiator fundamentals don't capture.
cases.false_positives_at_the_time: Two of the closest same-era look-alikes, both pursuing the identical "we are the AI/deep-learning datacenter chip" story in 2015-2016: (1) AMD -- same core GPU hardware category, launched its own datacenter GPU compute push (FirePro/Radeon Instinct-era positioning) in this window, but lacked an equivalent software ecosystem (ROCm never achieved comparable deep-learning-framework adoption to CUDA) and AMD's re-rating did not arrive on this narrative -- its subsequent rally was driven by CPU (Ryzen) execution and, later, crypto demand, not the AI-datacenter story. (2) Intel -- acquired Nervana Systems (Aug 2016) and Movidius (Sept 2016) explicitly to compete for the same AI-chip opportunity, with public statements nearly identical in substance to NVIDIA's ("AI is the next big wave"), backed by a far larger balance sheet; Intel's stock did not re-rate on this basis, and the acquired Nervana product line was later shelved in favor of Habana Labs' chips. Both are documented, verifiable false positives from the same 2015-2016 window: same narrative category, same claimed market, no comparable re-rating. I could not verify (session budget exhausted on WebSearch, and the specific pages 403'd on WebFetch) two other signals commonly cited in retrospectives -- a Jefferies note reportedly citing ~193% YoY datacenter growth off a 12%-of-revenue base, and a Roth Capital Partners upgrade citing named cloud customers -- so I have deliberately excluded those from the verified signals list rather than launder search-snippet claims into fact.

This was the FIRST public mention of Zen -- confirmed absent from the prior FY2014 10-K (filed Feb 2015).

This filing landed almost exactly at the trough (stock traded near its 2016 low the same week) -- it is the document that most directly poses the 'is this a real re-rating or a value trap' question the task is asking about.

signals.name: Mid-run confirmation (NOT a leading signal -- flagged explicitly): Aug 30, 2016 GlobalFoundries Wafer Supply Agreement Sixth Amendment let AMD dual-source 14nm/7nm wafers outside GF, and Mubadala's investment arm took a 75M-share warrant struck at $5.98 rather than cash -- a sophisticated, deeply-informed counterparty accepting equity risk near the market price just as the thesis was starting to play out
signals.evidence: Verified via direct WebFetch of the primary 8-K filed by AMD on 8/31/2016: Sixth Amendment dated Aug 30, 2016 gave AMD a limited waiver to use outside foundries for 14/7nm, set rising annual wafer targets through 2020, AMD paid GF $100M in installments; separately AMD issued West Coast Hitech (Mubadala) a warrant for 75,000,000 shares at $5.98/share expiring Feb 29, 2020 (max 50M exercisable in year one, Mubadala capped at 19.99% ownership), a ~$335M one-time Q3'16 charge. This happened 8 months AFTER the trough, so it is presented here as a mid-run reinforcing catalyst a real-time 8-K watcher would have caught -- not as something knowable 6-18 months before the run began. Included because it is exactly the kind of 'smart counterparty accepts equity/optionality instead of cash' signal the task is asking me to look for, just dated correctly.
signals.free_source: SEC EDGAR (8-K + exhibits, free, real-time)

cases.what_fundamentals_alone_missed: Standard fundamental analysis in 2014-2015 would have screened AMD OUT, correctly: shrinking R&D dollars ($1.4B in 2012 -> $1.1B in 2014 -> ~$0.9B in 2015, verified from the FY2015 10-K), a net-loss income statement, $2.2-2.26B of debt against a ~$1.6B market cap, and credit ratings in the CCC+/Caa1 (near-default) band -- by every conventional value or quality-growth screen this was a company fundamentals said to avoid or short. What fundamentals-only analysis structurally cannot price is optionality: whether a single, discrete, falsifiable technical bet (Zen hitting its stated 40% IPC target and shipping on the CEO's stated 2016/2017 schedule) would re-rate a company whose income statement looked terminal. The signals that actually mattered were forward-looking and binary -- an architecture disclosure with specific, checkable performance claims (May 2015), a CEO willing to reaffirm a hard date on an earnings call after her chief architect quit (Oct 2015), and later a sophisticated related-party (Mubadala/GF) accepting warrants instead of cash in a way that only makes sense if they believed in the roadmap. None of that shows up in a DCF or a ratio screen; it shows up in reading investor-day transcripts, earnings-call Q&A, and 8-K exhibits for the specific claim and then tracking whether it slipped. Short interest (~25% of float) is a related but separate axis: it explains why the move was violent (a squeeze) once the fundamental thesis started to be validated, but by itself it is not evidence the thesis was correct -- plenty of heavily-shorted distressed names never squeeze because the bear case is simply right.
cases.false_positives_at_the_time: The task's framing (quantum/robotics bets today) maps onto AMD's actual 2015-2018 near-neighbor: other chipmakers making the identical bet -- "beat Intel's x86 server monopoly with a new architecture" -- at the same time, most of which failed. Verified via WebSearch/summary of trade-press coverage: Qualcomm's Centriq ARM server SoC (sampled late 2016, effectively killed when its HuaXinTong China JV wound down by April 2019), Applied Micro's X-Gene ARM server line (sold off, later re-emerged as a separate startup, Ampere), Cavium's ThunderX/ThunderX2 (shipped, reached the market, but never scaled share and Cavium was absorbed into Marvell), and Broadcom's Vulcan ARM-server project (killed outright). All of these had comparable 2015-2017 narratives -- new architecture, server-market ambition, skeptical incumbent-defender analysts -- and all failed to dislodge Intel, unlike AMD's x86-compatible, drop-in-replacement Zen/EPYC bet. On the sell-side itself: mainstream coverage stayed bearish deep into the move -- Bank of America (Vivek Arya) is reported to have reiterated an Underperform rating on AMD in 2015 on the view that AMD faced 'structural challenges from Intel in PC and data center, and from Nvidia in discrete graphics' (found via WebSearch summary, not independently opened this session, so held at lower confidence) -- meaning consensus sell-side sentiment itself was a false signal (bearish) through much of the run-up, and would have been actively misleading to follow.

cases.sector_theme: Residential solar hardware / module-level power electronics (microinverters) — energy-transition small-cap that pre-dated the 2020 "solar bubble"

Verified: closing price was $0.85 on 2017-06-30 (10-K cover page) and the stock gained 52.8% in Jan 2019 alone after a rough 2H-2018, then +222% YTD by May 2019 (Motley Fool). Caveat: by SEC-filed market-cap snapshots, ENPH was still only ~$589M (non-affiliate value, 2018-06-30) — a small/mid-cap, not yet "large cap" (commonly >$10B) — as of mid-2018. The actual crossing into large-cap territory (multi-billion, eventually >$10B) happened in 2020, one year after this task's stated window; treat "2018-2019 run" as the setup phase whose fundamentals were laid down, with the large-cap outcome materializing slightly later than the prompt's framing implies.
cases.price_move: $0.85/share (close, 2017-06-30, SEC 10-K cover page) → 52.8% single-month gain in Jan 2019 → +222% YTD by May 2019 (Motley Fool) → roughly $25-28/share by end-2019 → >$100 by 2020-2021, i.e., on the order of 100x+ from the 2017 low to the eventual peak.

cases.what_fundamentals_alone_missed: A pure fundamentals screen (P/E, net margin, ROE, distress scores) would have screened ENPH OUT in 2017-2018: GAAP net losses persisted through FY2018 (-$45.2M in 2017, -$11.6M in 2018) and the company had carried a going-concern opinion only one year earlier. What fundamentals-alone missed was the *trajectory and structure* of the improvement: (1) the going-concern doubt was explicitly and formally lifted (a binary, dated, public flag), (2) operating income (not net income) had already flipped positive on an operating basis even while GAAP net income stayed negative, (3) a five-year exclusive anchor-supply contract with SunPower locked in ~$65M of high-margin (34%) revenue that wasn't yet in trailing financials, and (4) a management change put an operations-cost specialist in the CEO seat right before the cost-down product cycle (IQ6→IQ7) compressed COGS. None of that shows up as a ratio on last year's income statement — it shows up in 8-Ks, contract announcements, and forward guidance language, which is exactly the "probability of eventual success" layer the requester is describing as missing from fundamentals-only screens.
cases.false_positives_at_the_time: Several other beaten-down, sub-$2 solar/component microcaps carried a similar "left for dead, maybe a turnaround" story in 2017 without ENPH's specific combination of signals (going-concern lifted + anchor exclusive contract + operating-income inflection + management change) — e.g., Real Goods Solar, SPI Energy, and Ascent Solar remained penny stocks through this period and did not re-rate. SunPower itself — ironically the anchor customer whose contract was one of ENPH's strongest signals — kept struggling for years and later underwent a distressed restructuring/bankruptcy in 2024. I have not WebFetch-verified financial detail on these specific peer companies this session (this paragraph is inferred from general market history, not a page I opened), so treat it as a lower-confidence, illustrative comparison rather than a sourced claim on par with the ENPH signals above.

cases.what_fundamentals_alone_missed: A standard fundamentals screen in 2018-2019 would have flagged TSLA as low-quality and screened it OUT: a decade of GAAP losses, thin-to-negative net margins, heavy debt-funded capex, a CEO under an SEC fraud settlement (the Aug-2018 'funding secured' tweet), and a going-concern narrative loud enough that it was the single most-shorted stock on Wall Street by dollar value. What that lens could not price: (1) optionality on a platform shift — FSD software/OTA updates and eventual robotaxi economics are a call option on a margin structure that doesn't exist yet, not a line item a DCF on car gross margin will find; (2) execution/capacity signals that lead revenue by 6-12 months — Gigafactory Shanghai going from groundbreaking to shipped cars in under a year was visible in construction and delivery data well before it appeared in trailing financials; (3) reflexivity — a rising share price lowered Tesla's cost of capital, letting it raise the May-2019 $2.35B non-dilutive-feeling capital cheaply and fund the next capacity leg, a feedback loop invisible to static ratios; (4) pure market-structure mechanics — a ~23%-of-float short base created forced-buying energy once the loss narrative broke, and the Dec-2020 S&P 500 inclusion forced an estimated ~$51B of index/passive buying with zero connection to that quarter's fundamentals. Fundamentals told you Tesla was executing (Shanghai, margins, cash) — they never told you the multiple would go from single-digit-x sales to the richest in the auto industry; that repricing was a probability-of-becoming-the-category-winner bet the income statement cannot express.
cases.false_positives_at_the_time: Nikola (NKLA) is the clean, verifiable false positive: it went public via a June-2020 SPAC merger, its market cap more than doubled to ~$30B in the week after listing, and a September-2020 GM partnership (GM taking an ~11% stake, ~$2B) sent shares up another 40% — a near-identical 'the next Tesla' narrative arc (EV manufacturer, marquee industrial partner, no meaningful trailing revenue) running in real time just months after Tesla's own re-rating. Hindenburg Research's 15-Sep-2020 report (which I opened directly) alleged the company was 'an intricate fraud built on dozens of lies,' including a promotional video of the 'Nikola One' truck that was towed down a hill and presented as self-powered, and battery-technology claims Hindenburg called vaporware. The structural tell in hindsight: Tesla had shipping, revenue-generating products (Model 3/S/X) and a factory built and running in under a year (Shanghai) — hard, checkable capacity/delivery data — whereas Nikola's 'production' claims were demo-video and partnership-announcement narrative with no equivalent checkable capacity build. Background context I have NOT independently verified this session (flag as lower-confidence/unchecked): the broader 2020-21 EV-SPAC wave (Fisker, Lordstown Motors, Canoo, Workhorse, Faraday Future) that carried similar narratives and mostly underperformed or collapsed — I'm naming them from general knowledge, not from a page opened this session, so treat that list as a lead to verify, not a confirmed fact.

cases.what_fundamentals_alone_missed: Fundamentals alone (trailing GAAP revenue growth and net income) were actively misleading in this window: US commercial revenue growth was decelerating through 2022 (from 102% YoY in FY2021 to the 12-37% range by late 2022, per the verified 8-K releases), and full-year 2022 GAAP net income was still -$371M -- a naive screen would have flagged PLTR as a decelerating, unprofitable, "expensive" story, which is exactly what Morgan Stanley's sell-side Underweight said for two straight years. What fundamentals could not price in: (1) customer-count growth outpacing dollar growth (an expansion/optionality signal, not a revenue signal), (2) a live, contested-environment product proof in Ukraine that no peer had, (3) a GTM machine (bootcamps) already built and running before the demand wave arrived, and (4) the market's willingness to re-rate the whole cohort on a generative-AI narrative the instant ChatGPT made "enterprise AI" a buyable theme -- a multiple-expansion event, not an earnings event. In other words: fundamentals told you the company was becoming less bad, not that it was about to become the market's flagship AI bet.
cases.false_positives_at_the_time: C3.ai and BigBear.ai are the clean look-alikes: both rode the identical 2023 ChatGPT/enterprise-AI narrative and both re-rated hard (C3.ai +255% in 2023 per the Nasdaq.com piece), but their fundamentals did not follow -- C3.ai's FY2023 total revenue was ~$72.4M, "nearly flat" YoY, with widening GAAP losses per-share; BigBear.ai's revenue "stayed nearly flat in 2023 and only grew 2% in 2024" and it remained GAAP-unprofitable, compounded by its top customer's (Virgin Orbit) bankruptcy (verified via WebFetch of the 2025-10-12 Motley Fool comparison article). SoundHound AI also rallied on the same theme while staying GAAP-unprofitable with compressing gross margins. The distinguishing tell available at the time (not just in hindsight) was that Palantir's customer count, government contract wins, and the Q4 2022 GAAP profitability inflection were real and filed with the SEC, whereas the look-alikes' revenue lines stayed flat through the same period -- so the differentiator was checkable in the 10-Ks/10-Qs, it just required looking at customer/logo growth and segment mix rather than headline revenue-growth-YoY, which is where a fundamentals-only screen would have lumped all four names together as "story stocks."

cases.what_fundamentals_alone_missed: The FY2021/FY2022 10-Ks show a genuinely well-run, profitable, accelerating niche server OEM (46% revenue growth, expanding margins, no red flags in customer concentration) — but that same profile, read in isolation, does not distinguish SMCI from larger diversified server OEMs (Dell, HPE, Lenovo) that had the identical Nvidia GPU-server product lines yet barely re-rated in 2023 because AI servers were too small a slice of their total mix. Nothing in the filings quantifies the coming step-function: that ChatGPT-driven hyperscaler capex would make GPU-accelerated systems >50% of incremental industry demand, that SMCI's modular "Building Block" architecture gave it faster time-to-market on each new Nvidia GPU generation than the giants, or that gross margin would jump ~300bp on mix shift. That gap — relative speed-to-market and design-win share with Nvidia's newest platforms versus larger, slower-moving competitors — mostly shows up in earnings-call commentary, channel checks, and Nvidia's own datacenter-revenue disclosures, not in SMCI's balance sheet or income statement.
cases.false_positives_at_the_time: Dell Technologies and HPE carried the same Nvidia GPU-server product lines and comparable "AI infrastructure" language in their filings, but AI servers were too small a percentage of their overall revenue to move either stock in 2023 — both only began a much smaller re-rating later. Smart Global Holdings (now Penguin Solutions) — via its Penguin Computing division — is the closest small-cap look-alike: hyperscaler-facing, GPU/memory-adjacent infrastructure, similar "AI factory" narrative, yet it did not deliver anywhere close to SMCI's multiple expansion in 2023. I was not able, within this session's search budget, to independently verify a specific small-cap "AI server" name that carried an identical narrative and then collapsed to zero or near-zero — rather than invent one, I'm flagging that as an open gap in this research pass.

cases.what_fundamentals_alone_missed: A trailing-EPS or GAAP-profitability screen would have thrown VRT out or flagged it as low quality right before the run: FY2022 GAAP net income was positive ($76.6M per the earnings-release income statement I opened) but diluted EPS attributable to common stockholders was negative, $(0.04), because a large preferred-stock dividend accrual (a legacy of Vertiv's 2020 SPAC merger and its post-Emerson-carve-out capital structure) sat between net income and EPS. Fundamentals-as-reported (revenue, margin, EPS) also lag the actual demand signal by design -- the leading indicators that mattered (backlog, book-to-bill, named hyperscale customers, and the language shift from 'end-market demand' to explicit 'AI investment') all sit in the MD&A/press-release qualitative text and the order/backlog line, not in the income statement, and they were visible 6-17 months before the stock re-rated. Fundamentals alone also can't distinguish 'backlog inflated by supply-chain hoarding' (the bear case Vertiv itself raised repeatedly in 2022 guidance language about 'difficult comps' and 'order normalization') from 'backlog reflecting a durable structural shift to AI-driven compute density' -- that distinction was genuinely ambiguous in real time and only resolved once 2023 orders/margins kept beating quarter after quarter.
cases.false_positives_at_the_time: (1) The insider Form 4 cluster on 2022-12-19 (13 filings) is a textbook false positive if you count filings instead of reading transaction codes -- verified above to be routine $0 dividend-equivalent RSU accruals, not buying. (2) VRT's own 2021 pattern was a warning against pattern-matching the 2023 move too early: the stock ran from ~$20 to ~$28 in H1 2021 on general "digital infrastructure" enthusiasm, then fell 71% from its 2021 high to the June 2022 low of $8.22 as rates rose and margin fears took over -- an investor extrapolating 2021's rally into 2022 would have been wrong for a full year before being right in 2023. (3) I could not independently verify, within this session's search budget, whether look-alike diversified thermal/electrical suppliers exposed to the same hyperscale buildout (e.g., larger diversified industrials with data-center exposure) failed to re-rate the way VRT did in 2023 -- this is a plausible mechanism (VRT's 'pure-play data-center infrastructure' framing vs. a diversified peer's blended end-market mix) but I'm flagging it as an unverified inference, not a checked fact, because I ran out of WebSearch budget mid-session and did not manage to WebFetch a comparable peer's filings/price history to confirm it.

cases.what_fundamentals_alone_missed: A pure GAAP/quant fundamentals screen would have flagged NBIS as junk, not opportunity: FY2024 net loss from continuing operations of $396.9M, adjusted EBITDA loss of $266.4M, and explicit management/20-F language that the business "has never been profitable and may never reach profitability" (SEC 20-F, filed Apr 30, 2025). A P/E- or ROE-based screen returns nothing usable on a company with negative earnings. What fundamentals-alone missed was everything forward-looking and contract-driven: (1) the ARR guidance trajectory (Dec-2024 $90M -> guided $750M-$1B by Dec-2025, later beaten at $1.2B+) is a leading indicator that shows up in trailing financial statements only 1-2 quarters after the fact; (2) the credibility signal of Nvidia taking a direct equity stake alongside a capacity build-out, which is a qualitative/strategic tell with no line item on an income statement; (3) the optionality of a discrete, lumpy, binary contract event (the Microsoft $17.4B deal) that can reprice the stock 40-60% in a single session — this is a catalyst/event-probability question, not a valuation-multiple question; and (4) balance-sheet composition (cash as % of market cap, asset-light financing via customer prepayments funding 50-60% of capex per later reporting) that differentiates survivability within a cohort of similarly loss-making neocloud peers. Fundamentals told you the company was burning cash and unprofitable — accurately — but said nothing about the probability that a hyperscaler would sign a multi-billion-dollar capacity contract, which is precisely the kind of signal the user is asking to model for the next sector (quantum/robotics).
cases.false_positives_at_the_time: Being honest about hindsight: most of the obvious "look-alikes" in the pre-profit, heavy-capex, story-driven AI-infrastructure/neocloud cohort during this same period — CoreWeave, IREN, Applied Digital, Core Scientific, TeraWulf — did NOT cleanly fail; nearly all of them also re-rated sharply higher during 2025 as the broader neocloud/AI-capex theme ran (verified via a Jul 16, 2026 Yahoo Finance retrospective on a later sector-wide selloff, which describes CoreWeave, IREN, and Applied Digital all having posted large prior gains before that later correction). This is an important, honest limitation: I could not this session verify a clean, dated example of a name that looked structurally identical to NBIS 6-18 months out and then decisively failed (as opposed to being merely more volatile). The one differentiator I could verify directly is capital-structure quality: reporting describes Nebius's financing as comparatively "asset-light" (customer prepayments funding an estimated 50-60% of capex tied to major contracts) versus peers described as "capital-intensive, debt- and dilution-heavy" (CoreWeave, the bitcoin-miner-pivot names) — a real, findable-in-advance distinguishing signal, though I sourced this comparison from search-result synthesis rather than a primary filing I opened myself this session, so treat it as inferred, medium-confidence, not verified fact. Applied Digital (APLD) is the closest thing to a volatility-based cautionary tale I could substantiate directly: stockanalysis.com (opened this session) shows APLD carrying a 5.73 beta and a "44% plunge" cited by Forbes, i.e., an investor applying the same "bumper" heuristic to APLD would have needed to survive much larger drawdowns than an NBIS holder — but APLD was NOT a failure either (also up materially over the period); it is a higher-variance version of the same trade, not evidence the pattern-matching approach would have picked a loser.

cases.what_fundamentals_alone_missed: Every trailing financial-statement metric available 6-18 months out screamed "distressed, commodity bitcoin miner," not "future AI hyperscaler counterparty": FY2023 net loss of $171.9M narrowing to a still-negative $29.0M in FY2024 (20-F filed 2024-08-28), revenue still ~90%+ bitcoin mining (a halving-exposed, margin-volatile commodity business), and AI Cloud Services revenue running at only ~$5.85M for the six months to Dec 31 2024 (about $11.7M annualized) against total FY2024 revenue of $187.2M. A pure P/E, P/S, or EV/EBITDA screen would have flagged nothing distinguishing IREN from any other lossmaking small-cap bitcoin miner. What actually mattered was forward-looking, non-GAAP, real-asset optionality that only shows up in operational 6-K disclosures and site-level detail, not the income statement: contracted megawatts (2,310MW secured by Oct 2024), acreage, GPU counts and generation (H100 -> H200 -> Blackwell GB200 roadmap), and depth of the NVIDIA relationship (Cloud Partner Program, joint GTC appearances with customers like Poolside). Fundamentals told you the company was surviving; they could not price the option on power-constrained AI capacity that the market only woke up to in mid-to-late 2025.
cases.false_positives_at_the_time: Two distinct kinds of false positive existed. (1) A bearish one: Culper Research's July 2024 short report argued the AI-cloud buildout-cost claims were understated by 10-20x and that the legacy mining business was worth near-zero post-halving -- a well-evidenced, publicly available skeptical case that knocked the stock down ~20% in a day and would have kept a fundamentals-only investor out of the name for the subsequent ~900%+ move (confirmed via the opened Bitget News summary of the report; I could not open Culper's own report text, which returned an HTTP 403, so I cannot independently verify every claim attributed to it beyond the news summary). (2) A look-alike-sector one: several other bitcoin miners ran the identical "we're pivoting excess power/land into AI/HPC hosting" narrative in the same 2023-2024 window (the retrospective piece I opened names Bitfarms and Hive Digital as having jumped on comparable AI/cloud deal news in the same October 2025 window IREN was accelerating). I was not able to verify this session, via a page I actually opened, which specific same-era look-alikes underperformed or failed outright -- my attempts to fetch comparison pages (English Wikipedia on Applied Digital, DataCenterDynamics) returned 404/403 errors, and I ran out of WebSearch budget before finding a substitute source. That is a genuine gap in this research, not a claim I'm making from memory: I flag it rather than assert specific failed comparables I haven't verified.

cases.what_fundamentals_alone_missed: Trailing financials were unambiguously bad and got worse into the run: net loss widened from $44.6M (FY2023) to $149.3M (FY2024) to a 9-month FY2025 loss of $178.5M; revenue was concentrated in one or two customers (62% then 83% combined); the company carried going-concern language in its April 2025 10-Q and funded itself with dilutive/high-cost instruments (ATM equity, a $250M SEPA, and a 9%-coupon preferred). Any standard quality/profitability/leverage screen would rank Applied Digital as a distressed micro-cap to avoid. What that screen cannot price is optionality on a capacity/contract-backlog metric that doesn't appear in trailing GAAP statements: megawatts under letter-of-intent converting into definitive, 15-year, take-or-pay leases with investment-grade counterparties (CoreWeave, and later hyperscalers financed alongside Macquarie's multi-billion-dollar commitment). The re-rating was a bet on contract conversion and counterparty credit quality, not on the income statement in front of you — exactly the "how successful could this become" question the task frames fundamentals as unable to answer.
cases.false_positives_at_the_time: The cleanest, directly-evidenced false positive is Applied Digital's own earlier cycle: in May 2023 the stock (then still associated with its bitcoin-mining legacy) rallied hard (monthly close hit $8.37 in May 2023, $9.58 in July 2023) purely on the "we're pivoting to AI/HPC cloud" narrative, then fell roughly 40% within weeks after Wolfpack Research's July 6, 2023 report calling it "an embarrassing and predictable stock promotion" and flagging that insiders/B. Riley-affiliated parties controlled ~48.4% of the company. A momentum or narrative-only buyer in mid-2023 would have been badly whipsawed by a story that, superficially, looked identical to the 2025 thesis that eventually worked. Separately, even the "real" 2024 signals (the July 2024 exclusivity extension and the September 2024 private placement) produced a rally to $8.78-$10.94 by Sept-Nov 2024 that fully round-tripped back down to $3.31 by April 2025 before the sustained move began — showing that having the right signal did not by itself de-risk the entry timing. Beyond APLD itself, my working (lower-confidence, NOT independently source-verified this session because the WebSearch budget was exhausted before I could open primary documents on peers) understanding is that several other crypto-miner-to-AI-pivot names pursued similar letter-of-intent-stage HPC hosting narratives over 2023-2024 with mixed and slower conversion into hyperscaler-anchored, investment-grade, multi-year leases; I explicitly do not present specific peer names as confirmed failures here since I could not open a primary source on them before the search budget ran out — that gap should be treated as an open item, not a finding.

cases.what_fundamentals_alone_missed: CoreWeave was unprofitable every year available (net losses of $31M in 2022, $594M in 2023, $863M in 2024, per the S-1) and, being private until March 2025, had no trailing P/E, no public 10-K/10-Q history, no analyst estimates, no 13F holder base, no short-interest data, and no Form 4 insider-trading history for the entire pre-run window -- every classic fundamentals/equity-market screen (value, quality, momentum-on-price) returns nothing on a private company. What separated CoreWeave from other AI-infra hopefuls was not a ratio but a set of forward/contractual and credit-market signals fundamentals cannot see: (1) a hyperscaler (Microsoft) willing to commit to 62% of a company's revenue and co-sign de facto demand, (2) institutional debt markets underwriting $2.3B against literal GPUs as collateral 19 months before the float -- a bet on residual asset value, not earnings, (3) RPO/backlog ($15.1B) running ~8x trailing annual revenue, and (4) repeated, rapid private-mark-ups by sophisticated late-stage investors (Coatue, Fidelity, BlackRock, PIMCO) who had access to the data-room financials retail/fundamental screens never see. Fundamentals could describe the balance-sheet fragility (thin equity cushion, heavy leverage, customer concentration) but could not price the probability that Microsoft/OpenAI-driven GPU demand would keep outrunning supply.
cases.false_positives_at_the_time: Several 2023-2024 "AI infrastructure" names told a superficially identical story -- pivot hardware/compute capacity toward AI, raise big money against future demand -- and did not replicate CRWV's run, or only did so much later/partially: bitcoin miners that pivoted to AI/HPC hosting (Core Scientific, Applied Digital, Iris Energy/IREN) carried the same "GPU-backed capex, no near-term profit" profile but lacked CoreWeave's hyperscaler-anchor contract depth (62% revenue from one customer) and RPO scale, and traded on much noisier bitcoin-correlated narratives; AI-chip startups pursuing the same "raise against future demand" playbook (Cerebras, SambaNova, Graphcore) either withdrew/delayed their IPOs (Cerebras filed for IPO in 2024, withdrew in 2025, re-filed in April 2026) or stayed private for years, showing that "GPU/AI infra hype + big funding round" alone was not sufficient -- the discriminator in hindsight looks like it was the combination of a signed hyperscaler MSA generating >$1B in already-recognized revenue plus asset-backed debt markets already treating the compute fleet as investment collateral, not the capex story by itself.

cases.what_fundamentals_alone_missed: On every conventional fundamental multiple, IonQ looked absurd throughout 2023-2024: ~$22M of 2023 revenue against a market cap already in the billions (P/S well over 100x before the run even started), a $157.8M annual net loss, no path to GAAP profitability disclosed anywhere in the 10-K, and revenue small enough that a discounted-cash-flow or comparable-multiple model could not justify the pre-run valuation, let alone the post-run one. A fundamentals-only screen would have (correctly, on survival grounds) flagged the cash burn and (correctly, on valuation grounds) flagged the price as disconnected from current earnings power — and would have been right about that gap getting wider, not narrower, through the run. What it structurally cannot do is size the probability or the magnitude of a category-defining re-rating driven by: (1) a hyperscaler's own technical announcement (Google's Willow chip, Dec 9, 2024) validating the entire quantum-computing category as investable, which is a competitor event, not an IonQ fundamental; (2) reflexive short covering in a ~20%-of-float short name once the category caught a bid; (3) retail/social attention cascading across all quantum tickers simultaneously (IONQ, RGTI, QBTS all moved together, including names with far worse fundamentals — see Rigetti below); (4) the fact that IonQ's *forward* pipeline metric (bookings, a company-defined non-GAAP figure) was growing faster than GAAP revenue and was the number the bull case was actually pricing, not trailing income-statement profitability. Fundamental analysis bounds downside/survival risk well; it does not price a narrative re-rating, and it cannot distinguish, ex ante, which of several similarly unprofitable, similarly-narrated small caps in the same nascent category the market will anoint as the sector's investable proxy.
cases.false_positives_at_the_time: Rigetti Computing (RGTI) is the cleanest same-category look-alike: a March 2022 SPAC-merged, superconducting-qubit pure-play that by February 2023 had lost 93% of its SPAC-merger valuation and faced active Nasdaq delisting for trading near $0.90 — a much weaker fundamental picture than IonQ's growing revenue/bookings base — yet Rigetti rallied in the same Nov 2024-Jan 2025 quantum mania regardless, per contemporaneous coverage of the sector-wide move. That undercuts a clean "fundamentals separated the winner in real time" story: the market lifted the weaker balance sheet too, at least for the duration of the mania. Arqit Quantum (ARQQ) is the cautionary precedent rather than a name that ran alongside IonQ: it is a same-vintage quantum SPAC whose 2021-2022 "binding revenue contract" and "live customer" claims were later the subject of securities-fraud litigation alleging the underlying "customers" were actually grant-givers with no real product deployment — a public warning, well before 2023-2024, that unaudited customer/contract language from a pre-revenue quantum SPAC needs independent verification (which IonQ's AFRL and Hyundai disclosures could actually pass, and Arqit's reportedly could not). Neither comparison is airtight hindsight-proof: I could not verify, from a page I opened, that a contemporaneous 2023/2024 analyst report explicitly ran this exact IonQ-vs-Rigetti-vs-Arqit comparison at the time — the comparison here is my own reconstruction from primary filings/litigation records, not a retrieved period piece making the same argument.

cases.what_fundamentals_alone_missed: Every income-statement and balance-sheet metric available before the run pointed to distress, not a 30x move: quarterly revenue stuck at $2-3M, quarterly net losses of $12-21M, a stock under Nasdaq's $1.00 minimum-bid rule with a live delisting clock, and a balance sheet being kept alive by dilutive ATM sales and an 11%+ venture loan (all verified in 10-Qs/8-Ks above). None of that predicted the trigger: two exogenous, sector-wide narrative events in Dec 2024 (Google's Willow chip claim and Amazon's Quantum Embark program) that re-rated the entire quantum group on speculative future total-addressable-market, not on Rigetti's own trailing financials. What fundamentals alone missed was the optionality value of an accumulated government/defense-lab relationship portfolio (AFRL IDIQ, UK NQCC) and a shipped on-prem hardware product (Novera QPU) — assets that were nearly worthless in current-period revenue terms but became the story once the market decided to price the sector on a 2030s TAM instead of 2024 sales. This is structurally the same failure mode fundamentals-only analysis has for any pre-revenue-inflection "bumper": DCF/multiple-based valuation is anchored to cash flows that don't exist yet, so it systematically cannot assign probability to a narrative catalyst it can't foresee.

cases.what_fundamentals_alone_missed: A pure fundamentals/multiples screen in Q3-Q4 2024 would have rejected QBTS outright: revenue was $1.9M and falling 27% YoY, bookings were falling 22% YoY, the company was running an Adjusted EBITDA loss on the order of $50M+/year, share count was continuously expanding via ATM offerings, and the SEC filings themselves stated a "history of losses" with "continuing losses for the foreseeable future." None of that was wrong -- it is still largely true. What it missed: (1) the segment decomposition (QCaaS recurring revenue +41% YoY hidden inside a falling headline number) that showed a real, if small, inflecting business under the hood; (2) a capacity/roadmap signal (the Jan-2024 Advantage2 prototype) that had zero revenue attached to it at the time but became the basis of a scientific-credibility claim ("quantum supremacy," Science, Mar 2025) that the market later paid for; (3) that the repricing was triggered by a category-level attention event (Google's Willow chip) completely exogenous to D-Wave's own P&L -- fundamentals cannot forecast a sector-wide sentiment catalyst; and (4) float/short-interest mechanics (an already-short, thinly-floated post-SPAC stock) that mechanically amplified whatever narrative arrived. In short, fundamentals correctly described how the company behaved (small, cash-burning, dilutive) but had no mechanism to price the probability of a narrative-driven, sector-wide repricing -- which is exactly the gap the user is asking the "super judge" layer to fill.
cases.false_positives_at_the_time: Quantum Computing Inc. (QUBT) and Rigetti Computing (RGTI) rallied in near-lockstep with QBTS off the same Dec-2024 Willow catalyst and were largely indistinguishable from QBTS on a pure "quantum-computing-theme" momentum screen. QUBT in particular had a materially weaker underlying profile: it is a renamed former consumer-beverage shell (Innovative Beverage Group Holdings) that executed a 1-for-200 reverse split in 2018 to remain listed, and its quarterly revenue was reported in the low hundreds of thousands of dollars -- an order of magnitude below QBTS's already-small book, with no equivalent of D-Wave's named Forbes Global 2000 customer list or FY2023 bookings inflection. Both QUBT and RGTI are documented to have carried recurring losses and dilution risk into and through the rally. The point for a forward-looking screen: at the time (Q4 2024), the differentiator between QBTS and its more fragile look-alikes was only visible to someone who opened the actual 8-Ks/10-Ks (bookings growth, named enterprise logos, an actual sold hardware unit) rather than someone screening purely on "quantum computing" sector momentum -- a screen on ticker-tag/theme alone would have sized QBTS and QUBT identically.

cases.what_fundamentals_alone_missed: Fundamentals alone would have screamed 'avoid': pre-revenue, ~$105M cumulative losses, explicit going-concern-style capital-risk language, a disclosed $550-650M unfunded capex gap, and a founder holding ~88% of voting power. No P/E, no P/S, negative free cash flow -- a standard quality/value screen ranks this as un-investable. What that framework structurally cannot price is optionality bundled with pre-committed distribution: a physics-validated technology (largest commercial phased array flown in LEO, live over-the-air voice/5G calls with unmodified phones), an accumulating patent moat (2,600+ claims), and -- critically -- anchor customers who were simultaneously equity/board-seat holders and the only entities that could supply the scarce input (spectrum) and the demand side (subscriber base). That combination converts a binary regulatory/technical-milestone bet into a real option whose payoff is nonlinear once milestones clear (FCC framework advances, satellites launch and work, a definitive commercial deal signs) -- which is exactly the May-September 2024 sequence that repriced the stock. A DCF or comp-multiple approach has no slot for 'the demand side of the two-sided market already bought equity and a board seat before there was revenue.'
cases.false_positives_at_the_time: The 2021-vintage SPAC 'New Space' cohort looked interchangeable with AST SpaceMobile through 2022-2023: Virgin Orbit (launch-vehicle operator) filed Chapter 11 on 2024-04-04 -- verified via its own SEC 8-K exhibit -- after failing to raise capital; Astra, Momentus and Spire Global all traded under $1 and drew exchange delisting notices in the same window (per WebSearch-only corroboration, not independently re-verified on a primary filing in this session); Redwire and BlackSky faced similar cash-burn/dilution pressure. A screen for 'cheap, disruptive, pre-revenue space stock' would have flagged all of them identically to ASTS in 2022-2023. The distinguishing feature a careful analyst could isolate at the time, without hindsight: AST SpaceMobile's counterparties were the actual distribution channel (mobile network operators holding spectrum and subscribers) and were contractually and financially bound in (revenue-share terms, board seats, and by January 2024 direct capital), whereas the failed peers were manufacturing/launch-service plays with no analogous locked-in demand side. That is a structural difference visible in the 10-K and 8-Ks well before the run, not a narrative told after the fact.

cases.what_fundamentals_alone_missed: A GAAP-fundamentals screen (P&L margin, EPS, YoY revenue growth-rate trend) would have scored RKLB poorly to neutral in the 6-18 month pre-run window: FY2023 revenue growth had decelerated sharply from FY2022 (+239% to +15.9%), and the company was burning ~$180M/year with no profitability in sight (confirmed FY2024 net loss was still -$190.2M despite revenue nearly doubling to $436.2M). What fundamentals-as-reported could not capture: (1) backlog is a leading indicator that sits off the income statement — the $1.0B+ signed-but-unrecognized backlog at Dec 2023 only started converting to reported revenue growth in the Aug-2024 quarter that kicked off the rally; (2) launch reliability/cadence and government-contract diversification (HASTE, Space Systems buses) are capability/moat signals with no direct P&L line item until they scale; (3) competitor attrition (Virgin Orbit's 2023 bankruptcy, Astra Space's near-collapse) reduced the credible-peer set, which a single-company fundamentals read never surfaces; (4) the market was pricing Neutron (the reusable medium-lift rocket) as a speculative, pre-revenue option — its de-risking (engine assembly, facility buildout) moved narrative and multiple long before it moved any reported number.
cases.false_positives_at_the_time: Verified this session: Virgin Orbit — a SPAC-merged, small-launch-vehicle peer that looked structurally similar to RKLB in 2021-2022 (same "de-SPAC space company" template, unprofitable, pre-scale) — filed for bankruptcy and liquidated in 2023; RKLB itself bought its Long Beach facility out of the bankruptcy auction. This is direct evidence that "looks like RKLB" was not sufficient — several same-era small-cap launch/space SPACs (commonly cited alongside Virgin Orbit: Astra Space, which underwent a reverse split and was taken private in 2024 at a fraction of its SPAC valuation) shared RKLB's profile (de-SPAC'd, pre-profit, speculative reusability/launch-cadence bets) and did not survive or re-rate the same way. cases.what_fundamentals_alone_missed: As of the last pre-run disclosure (10-Q filed 2024-08-14), Oklo had zero revenue, a $53.4M six-month net loss, an explicit management-authored going-concern doubt, no operating reactor, no NRC-approved design (its 2022 combined license application had been denied outright — per en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oklo_Inc.), and a first commercial unit not targeted until 2027. Every conventional fundamental metric (margins, ROIC, revenue growth, coverage ratios) said "avoid" or was simply undefined. None of that told you the stock was about to re-rate ~3x in a month, because the re-rating was not driven by a change in Oklo's own financials — it was driven by (1) a sector-wide macro catalyst (the Sept 20, 2024 Microsoft-Constellation Three Mile Island deal) that made "AI data centers need nuclear power" a tradeable theme overnight, and (2) Oklo's disproportionate share of narrative attention within that theme via the Sam Altman/OpenAI halo effect and the sheer breadth (GW-scale, if non-binding) of its LOI pipeline. Fundamentals describe survival risk and cash runway; they say nothing about which name in a nascent, pre-revenue sub-sector the market will anoint as the proxy for a newly-popular macro story.
cases.false_positives_at_the_time: NuScale Power (SMR) is the clearest look-alike. It had strictly better regulatory standing than Oklo going into the period — the NRC certified NuScale's 50 MWe VOYGR design in 2022 (the only certified SMR design in the US), whereas Oklo's own combined license application had been denied by the NRC in January 2022. Yet NuScale's flagship commercial project (the UAMPS/Carbon Free Power Project in Idaho) collapsed in November 2023 after cost estimates ballooned from $3.6B to $9.3B, forcing a joint termination and a 28% staff layoff (verified via en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NuScale_Power). Despite that real anchor-customer failure, NuScale's stock rallied almost in lockstep with Oklo's during the same window — $6.31 (2024-06-03) -> $8.25 (2024-09-16) -> $12.39 (2024-10-16) -> $17.93 (2024-12-16), roughly +184% over the same six months (verified via Yahoo Finance chart JSON for ticker SMR) — purely on the same sector-wide AI-power re-rating. An analyst who screened on "regulatory progress" or "an actual NRC-approved design" as the discriminating signal would have picked NuScale, and NuScale did rally too — but for reasons unrelated to its own commercial pipeline, which had just failed. This shows the theme itself, not company-specific fundamentals or even regulatory status, was doing most of the work in 2024; picking the single best performer within the basket required reading narrative concentration (Altman/OpenAI halo, LOI breadth) rather than balance sheets.

cases.what_fundamentals_alone_missed: Every trailing fundamental screen through 2023 said avoid: persistent large net losses (FY2024 net loss was -$359.75M per stockanalysis.com, and prior years were also unprofitable), revenue concentrated in one customer at 72% as recently as Q3 2023, and an active at-the-market share-sale facility that keeps diluting per-share value. None of that changed the day the stock re-rated. What a P&L-and-multiples view could not price in: (1) a backlog/bookings metric ($661M cumulative, 2x YoY, disclosed Feb 2024) that is a leading indicator invisible in trailing revenue; (2) rapid de-risking of customer concentration (72%→12% in a year) that fundamentally changes the risk profile of the same revenue base; (3) the pure attention/re-rating effect of a 13F disclosure making a years-old Nvidia stake newly visible to retail — a flow/narrative event with zero change to the underlying financials on the day it happened; and (4) M&A-driven vertical expansion (SYNQ3 into restaurants, Amelia into banking/insurance/healthcare) that shows up in reported financials only with a multi-quarter lag, so the strategic optionality was visible in 8-Ks well before it appeared in any reported ratio.

cases.peak_and_collapse: Went public via VectoIQ SPAC merger June 4, 2020; by June 9 shares had more than doubled and by month-end the company was valued near $13B on ~$80,000 of H1 2020 revenue (Wikipedia, citing contemporaneous reporting). Hindenburg Research's Sept 10, 2020 report ('an intricate fraud') triggered a 10% same-day drop, 36% by Sept 12; Trevor Milton resigned as Executive Chairman Sept 21, 2020 (stock -20% that day). Shares kept bleeding for years; Nikola filed Chapter 11 on Feb 19, 2025 with shares at $0.44, and by late 2025 the OTC-relisted NKLAQ traded near $0.007 -- roughly a 99.6% decline from its all-time (post-split-adjusted) high.
looked_like_a_winner_because: First-mover 'hydrogen-electric semi truck' narrative riding the 2020 EV/decarbonization wave, marketed as a Tesla-of-trucking
A named strategic partner: General Motors announced Sept 8, 2020 it would take an 11% equity stake (~$2B) and a board seat, and supply fuel cells/batteries
A large, headline-grabbing 'order book' (tens of thousands of reserved trucks) presented as demand validation
A viral Jan 2018 video appearing to show the Nikola One truck driving under its own power
Founder/CEO Trevor Milton's aggressive social-media promotion of imminent commercial hydrogen production and in-house tech

what_differed_and_was_knowable.signal: The 'Nikola One in motion' video (the core proof the truck worked) was independently falsifiable: it was filmed on a downhill grade after the truck was towed to the top, per former-employee text messages and an investigator's replication (56 mph reached rolling in neutral over 2.1 miles) -- and the underlying video had been public since Jan 2018.
what_differed_and_was_knowable.evidence: Hindenburg Research report, hindenburgresearch.com/nikola, published Sept 10, 2020: documents photos of an incomplete truck as late as Aug 2016 and the towed-downhill reconstruction of the Jan 2018 video.

what_differed_and_was_knowable.signal: GM's own diligence produced a visible signal within weeks: the announced 11%/$2B equity stake was eliminated entirely by Nov 30, 2020, leaving only an arms-length fuel-cell/battery supply agreement -- the 'smart money' partner walked from equity after looking under the hood.
what_differed_and_was_knowable.evidence: Nikola Corporation, Wikipedia (sourced to contemporaneous reporting): 'the equity stake was eliminated entirely... GM no longer would take an 11% ownership position' (Nov 30, 2020), preserving only the supply agreement.

what_differed_and_was_knowable.signal: SEC settlement (Dec 21, 2021, $125M penalty) formally confirmed the specific fabrications -- hydrogen cost/production claims, false in-house tech, inflated order/reservation counts -- but this is a LAGGING confirmation, not an early-warning signal: the market had already re-priced most of the fraud risk 15 months earlier off the Hindenburg report and Milton's resignation.
what_differed_and_was_knowable.evidence: SEC Press Release 2021-267 (Dec 21, 2021): Nikola to pay $125M for misleading investors about hydrogen production costs, in-house production capabilities, and truck reservations/orders.

cases.peak_and_collapse: Merged with DiamondPeak Holdings SPAC Oct 23, 2020 at an estimated $1.6B equity value. Hindenburg Research's March 12, 2021 report knocked the stock down 17% same-day; CEO Steve Burns and CFO Julio Rodriguez resigned June 14, 2021 after disclosing insufficient funds to reach commercial production. The stock continued to a near-total wipeout; the company filed Chapter 11 on June 27, 2023 (suing Foxconn over an unfunded $170M commitment), sold assets for $10M, and the shell later became Nu Ride Inc. then Stark Novus Financial Inc. (SNFI), now an unrelated financial shell trading around $1.71 -- the original EV business and its shareholders' value are gone.
looked_like_a_winner_because: Claimed ~100,000 'pre-orders' for the Endurance electric pickup, presented publicly as proof of overwhelming fleet demand
A repurposed unionized GM plant (Lordstown, Ohio) framed as an already-solved manufacturing/scale problem
Founder Steve Burns's credibility as a prior EV-truck founder (Workhorse) lent an experienced-operator narrative
A later 'white knight' partnership announced with Foxconn (Oct 2021) implying a well-capitalized manufacturing partner had underwritten the plan
SPAC-era retail enthusiasm for pure-play EV names with an imminent production date

what_differed_and_was_knowable.signal: The 100,000 'pre-orders' were shown to be largely non-binding letters of intent with zero deposit or purchase obligation, including a $735M/14,000-truck order from a Texas apartment-based entity (E Squared Energy) and a $52.5M order from a two-person startup using a UPS Store mailbox (Innervations LLC); Lordstown reportedly paid $30-50 per non-binding pre-order through consulting firms to inflate the count.
what_differed_and_was_knowable.evidence: Hindenburg Research report, hindenburgresearch.com/lordstown, published March 12, 2021: names the specific counterparties and their lack of operating substance, and describes the pay-per-order arrangement.

what_differed_and_was_knowable.signal: CEO and CFO resigned June 14, 2021 with the company explicitly disclosing it lacked sufficient capital to reach commercial production -- a funding-shortfall admission, not a vague 'personal reasons' departure -- roughly two years before the Chapter 11 filing.
what_differed_and_was_knowable.evidence: Lordstown Motors, Wikipedia (sourced to contemporaneous reporting): Burns and Rodriguez 'resigned June 14, 2021, following disclosure that the company lacked sufficient funds for commercial production.'

what_differed_and_was_knowable.signal: The company's own FY2020 10-K (filed March 25, 2021, the same month as the Hindenburg report) already carried going-concern risk-factor language warning that the value of an investment would be materially and adversely affected if the company could not continue as a going concern -- a self-disclosed, audited-filing signal available to any reader before the CEO resignation.
what_differed_and_was_knowable.evidence: Lordstown Motors 10-K for FY2020, filed with the SEC March 25, 2021 (accession 0001558370-21-003449): risk-factor section states 'If we were not able to continue as a going concern, or if there were doubt about our ability to do so, the value of your investment would be materially and adversely affected.'

cases.peak_and_collapse: Merged with Tortoise Acquisition Corp Oct 2020 (~$1.6B valuation). Within weeks, short-seller Bonitas Research (Oct 2020) alleged the same category of problem seen at NKLA/RIDE -- that only a portion of the 'customers' in investor presentations had actually purchased its Hybrid-X system. The stock fell from its SPAC-era highs to well under $1 through 2022-2023. UNLIKE the other three names, Hyliion did not go bankrupt: it discontinued its original hybrid-powertrain business in Nov 2023 (cutting headcount by two-thirds) and redeployed capital into the KARNO generator technology (acquired from GE Additive for $37M, Aug 2022), pivoting toward data-center/AI power demand. As of Sept 24, 2026 it trades at $4.20 (down ~50% from a 2026 high of $8.49, not from its original 2020 peak), market cap ~$750M, still listed on NYSE American -- the survivor case that most resembles what the user is trying to find prospectively.
looked_like_a_winner_because: Positioned as a 'picks-and-shovels' EV-adjacent play (hybrid electric powertrain retrofits for existing diesel fleets) rather than a full new-vehicle OEM, seen as lower execution risk
Investor presentations listing large fleet operators as customers, implying near-term commercial traction
SPAC-era momentum in the same 2020 EV wave as NKLA and RIDE
A credible, technically fluent founder-CEO (Thomas Healy) narrative around a genuinely patentable hybrid drivetrain

what_differed_and_was_knowable.signal: A short-seller report (Bonitas Research, Oct 2020) alleging inflated/unconverted customer claims appeared here too, within weeks of the SPAC close -- proving that 'a short report exists' is NOT by itself a discriminator between a bumper and a blow-up; NKLA, RIDE, and HYLN all got one.
what_differed_and_was_knowable.evidence: Hyliion, Wikipedia (sourced to contemporaneous reporting): Bonitas Research, Oct 2020, disputed that listed customers had 'actually purchased its Hybrid-X system' and challenged fuel-efficiency claims.

what_differed_and_was_knowable.signal: What differed is what management did next: rather than escalating claims to defend the falling stock, it spent $37M (Aug 2022) acquiring a real, GE-vetted generator technology (KARNO) as an exit ramp from the unproven original product -- a capital-allocation signal visible in the 8-K/press release, well before the original thesis fully died.
what_differed_and_was_knowable.evidence: Hyliion, Wikipedia: 'August 2022: Acquired KARNO generator technology from GE Additive for $37 million.'

what_differed_and_was_knowable.signal: The company killed the original, unfulfilled truck-electrification business outright in Nov 2023 (two-thirds workforce cut) rather than keep burning cash chasing orders that never converted -- a disclosed decision to stop funding a broken thesis, the mirror image of GOEV/RIDE/NKLA continuing to promise imminent commercialization until the cash ran out.
what_differed_and_was_knowable.evidence: Hyliion, Wikipedia: 'November 2023: Discontinued powertrain business and reduced workforce by two-thirds.'

cases.peak_and_collapse: Merged with Hennessy Capital Acquisition Corp IV Dec 22, 2020 at an anticipated $2.4B valuation. Trading collapsed over 2021-2024 amid repeated funding shortfalls, related-party controversy, and near-zero deliveries; Canoo furloughed its Oklahoma workforce and idled its factory in Dec 2024, then filed Chapter 7 bankruptcy Jan 17, 2025 with under $50,000 in disclosed assets. Now trades as GOEVQ on OTC pink sheets near $0.001, market cap ~$16K -- effectively total loss.
looked_like_a_winner_because: A modular 'skateboard' EV platform pitched across multiple vehicle classes (vans, pickups, lifestyle vehicles) as a capital-efficient, platform-based OEM story

A string of high-profile named customers/LOIs: Walmart (July 2022, 4,500 vehicles + 10,000-unit option), USPS pilot vehicles (Jan 2024), and binding-sounding orders from Kingbee and Zeeba (Oct 2022, thousands of light-duty vehicles)
A chairman/majority-backer, Tony Aquila (AFV Partners), publicly positioned as a hands-on operator willing to personally fund the company through downturns
SPAC-era EV enthusiasm plus a 2020-2021 IPO-adjacent valuation of $2.4B

what_differed_and_was_knowable.signal: Governance concentration was visible at the moment it happened: on April 22, 2021 co-founder/CEO Ulrich Kranz stepped down and board chairman and largest investor Tony Aquila (via AFV Partners) installed himself as CEO -- collapsing the independent-oversight/operator separation that normally checks a controlling shareholder.
what_differed_and_was_knowable.evidence: Canoo, Wikipedia (sourced to contemporaneous reporting): 'April 22, 2021 - Co-founder/CEO Ulrich Kranz stepped down; Tony Aquila assumed CEO role.'

what_differed_and_was_knowable.signal: Canoo directly disclosed in May 2022 that it had funding for less than one additional quarter of operations -- a quantified, audited-filing going-concern admission, not boilerplate risk-factor language, roughly 2.5 years before the actual Chapter 7 filing.
what_differed_and_was_knowable.evidence: Canoo, Wikipedia (sourced to SEC disclosures/reporting): 'May 2022 - Disclosed insufficient funding for more than one quarter.'

what_differed_and_was_knowable.signal: The related-party structure flagged by the April 2021 CEO installation was confirmed in the FY2023 annual report: expenses paid to CEO Aquila's private company for aircraft and shared services were nearly four times Canoo's entire $886,000 net revenue for the year -- available in the audited 10-K roughly a year before bankruptcy.
what_differed_and_was_knowable.evidence: Canoo, Wikipedia (sourced to Canoo's 2023 annual report / 10-K): 'expenses paid to CEO Aquila's company for private aircraft and shared services were nearly four times' the company's $886,000 net revenue.

what_differed_and_was_knowable.signal: The headline customer deals were structurally weak or never performed: the Walmart deal (July 2022, 4,500 vehicles + 10,000-unit option) carried a 30-day termination clause, and across every announced order (Walmart, Kingbee, Zeeba, USPS) fewer than 12 vehicles had actually been delivered as of Oct 2024 -- a directly checkable delivery-count vs. announced-order-count gap, visible in each subsequent 10-Q rather than the press release.
what_differed_and_was_knowable.evidence: Canoo, Wikipedia (sourced to SEC filings/reporting): Walmart agreement 'included 30-day termination clause'; 'Actual Deliveries: Fewer than 12 vehicles delivered across all orders as of October 2024.'

discriminators: A short-seller/investigative report existing is NOT itself the discriminator -- NKLA, RIDE, and HYLN all attracted one within weeks of going public; what discriminates is whether the report's specific factual claims (staged demo footage, fabricated or paid-for orders, non-existent production capability) survive an independent check, versus being a legitimately early but real technology bet.

Binding vs. non-binding demand: treat every 'order,' 'pre-order,' or 'letter of intent' as worthless until you can confirm a deposit, a termination-clause-free contract, and -- most importantly -- actual delivered units in subsequent 10-Qs. RIDE's 100,000 'pre-orders' and GOEV's Walmart/Kingbee/Zeeba deals both looked identical to a real order book on a press release and were hollow (fewer than 12 GOEV vehicles ever delivered; RIDE orders traced to shell entities paid $30-50 each).

Watch what a co-investing 'smart money' strategic partner does with its OWN capital after diligence, not what it announces going in: GM cut its Nikola equity stake to zero within 12 weeks of the initial announcement while Foxconn's $170M Lordstown commitment was later the subject of a breach-of-contract suit -- both are dated, checkable, and preceded the ultimate collapse by years.

Governance concentration is a leading indicator, checkable the day it happens: a board chairman/largest shareholder installing himself as CEO (Canoo's Aquila, April 2021) removes the independent check that would normally catch related-party self-dealing -- later confirmed when Canoo's own 10-K showed payments to the CEO's private company at ~4x net revenue.

Quantified, audited-filing going-concern language beats narrative every time: boilerplate risk-factor going-concern language (Lordstown's March 2021 10-K) is nearly universal and low-signal; a SPECIFIC disclosed runway number (Canoo's May 2022 'funding for less than one quarter') is a hard, dated, near-term warning that reliably preceded bankruptcy by ~2-3 years across this cohort.

Executive/CFO departures explicitly tied to a disclosed funding gap (Lordstown's CEO+CFO, June 2021) are a much stronger signal than departures framed as 'personal reasons' or ordinary succession -- read the actual 8-K departure language, not just the fact of departure.

The single cleanest discriminator observed here is what management does AFTER the first credibility hit: Hyliion took a short-seller report in Oct 2020 just like NKLA and RIDE, but by 2022-2023 it killed its own unproven original product line, cut headcount, and bought a real, third-party-vetted technology (GE's KARNO) instead of escalating claims to defend the stock -- NKLA, RIDE, and GOEV all instead kept promising imminent commercialization until the cash ran out and management/customer claims kept getting more aggressive, not less.

SEC settlements, DOJ indictments/convictions, and Chapter 7/11 filings are LAGGING confirmations, not early-warning tools for a live 'bumper' search -- in every case here they landed 12-50+ months after the market had already re-priced most of the risk off short reports, executive departures, and funding disclosures. A live screening process has to weight the earlier, checkable operational/financial signals above, not wait for regulators.

None of this substitutes for fundamental analysis, but it also is not reducible to it: the discriminating signals above (order-book veracity, related-party structure, disclosed runway, and post-setback capital-allocation behavior) are things fundamental ratios do not capture directly and require reading primary filings/short reports rather than headline metrics.

discriminators: Read the filing, not the press release: a headline 'order' or 'letter of intent' can carry zero deposit and zero cancellation penalty (Arrival/UPS, FY2021 20-F). Pull the actual customer-contract risk-factor language before treating a named enterprise customer as a real revenue floor.

Cash runway is a number, not a vibe: divide disclosed total liquidity by the trailing operating burn rate from the same filing. If a 10-Q/10-K's own liquidity footnote conditions '12 months of runway' on continued access to an at-the-market or preferred-stock financing program, that is company-authored disclosure that survival already depends on further dilution (Luminar Q2 2025 10-Q: $107.6M liquidity vs $98M six-month burn).

Delinquent-filing notices (NT 10-K / NT 20-F) are an administrative tripwire that fires before the narrative catches up -- a company that cannot close its books on time is disclosing a problem months ahead of the eventual price move (Arrival, May 2023).

Explicit going-concern or material-weakness language in a filing is a bright-line, checkable fact, not sentiment -- search EDGAR full-text search for the ticker plus 'going concern' rather than relying on news coverage.

Founder/insider removal 'following an Audit Committee investigation into conduct' -- even with no further detail disclosed -- is one of the highest-value public red flags available: it is dated, filed, and precedes the eventual value destruction by a wide margin in both cases examined here (Velodyne Feb 2021, Luminar May 2025).

Loss of the flagship anchor customer/design win is a distinct, later-stage confirming signal from the funding-crisis signal, and the two often cluster within the same year rather than one long-lead indicator covering everything (Luminar: liquidity crisis Aug 2025 -> Volvo drops it as standard equipment Nov 2025 -> Chapter 11 Dec 2025).

Dilution/share-count trajectory over time matters more than the headline price: a stock can look 'cheap' after a crash while shares outstanding have grown multiples faster than any revenue base, meaning existing holders are being diluted into irrelevance even before bankruptcy.

A specific, falsifiable short-seller claim (not just 'this is a bubble' punditry) is worth checking against the filings regardless of the short-seller's track record, because the claim itself is a hypothesis you can verify with primary sources (QuantumScape/Scorpion Capital) -- but treat the short report's own text as unverified until you've read it directly, not just the fact that it was published.

None of these four collapses required fundamental analysis to see coming in the sense of a DCF -- they required reading Item 3 (Legal Proceedings), Item 5.02 (officer/director departures), the going-concern paragraph, and the customer-commitment risk factors in filings the companies themselves published while the stock still looked fine. That is exactly the 'super judge' function the requester is describing: an agent whose job is not to value the technology but to continuously diff each new filing against the last one for these specific tripwires.

Caveat on this research: two of the above evidentiary items (the Scorpion Capital report's specific allegations, and the details behind Austin Russell's ethics investigation) were corroborated only via Wikipedia's citation of a news headline, not by directly opening the primary article -- search engines and several news sites (TheStreet, Bing, DuckDuckGo) returned 403s, CAPTCHAs, or empty results to automated fetch this session. Treat those two specific sub-claims as reported/secondary, not independently confirmed, and re-verify against the primary article before relying on them.
