discriminators: An explicit, filed 'going concern' / substantial-doubt statement (10-K or 10-Q) is a bright-line legal disclosure, not boilerplate risk language — it showed up 4-5 months ahead of Virgin Orbit's and Astra's terminal events and is checkable every quarter for any name in this cohort.

Runway math, not just cash balance: cash ÷ trailing-quarter burn. Virgin Orbit's runway compressed from ~5 quarters to under 2 in a single 10-Q (cash $194.2M→$71.2M while 9-month burn rose $111.7M→$158.0M) — the rate of compression mattered more than the absolute cash figure.

Whether the load-bearing technical milestone underlying the revenue thesis actually succeeded on schedule, and what management did when it didn't: Astra didn't just have two launch failures, it discontinued the very rocket (Launch System 1) that generated its backlog four months before the going-concern disclosure — abandonment of the current product line is a stronger signal than the failure itself.

Backlog/contract language precision: 'signed contracts' with a dollar figure (Momentus's ~$33M) versus SPAC-deck total-addressable-market or reservation-list numbers (Virgin Galactic's ~600 ticket holders) — the gap between the two is a measure of how much of the story is still narrative.

Founder/executive departures tied to a structural or legal problem with the company itself (Momentus's Kokorich forced out over an undisclosed national-security issue, announced 7 months before the SPAC merger even closed) are knowable before the stock even starts trading under its new ticker — this is a pre-deal discriminator, not a post-IPO one.

Regulatory enforcement that directly falsifies the technology or customer claims underlying the valuation (SEC v. Momentus/Stable Road, settled a month before merger close) is categorically different from generic litigation risk — it invalidates the specific numbers retail investors were shown.

Insider-selling context matters more than the headline number: distinguish a full liquidation of a founder/sponsor's directly-held, liquid personal stake (Palihapitiya's Form 4s, sold to zero) from routine 10b5-1 diversification of a small percentage, and check what fraction of total economic interest (including separately-locked sponsor/founder shares) was actually exited.

Workforce reductions and their frequency: a single reduction is a cost-control measure, but one that lands within months of, and is later followed by, a going-concern disclosure (Astra: 16% cut in Nov 2022 → going-concern language four months later) functions as a leading indicator worth flagging in real time, not just in hindsight.

None of these four discriminators is visible on a price chart at the peak — ASTR, VORB, SPCE and MNTS all shared the same 2021 retail-mania price action as survivors in the same SPAC-space cohort; the separation only appears in filed disclosures (going-concern language, burn-rate trend, backlog wording, insider Form 4s, and abandonment of the flagship product), which is why this research treats price action as the thing to be explained, not the signal itself.

what_differed_and_was_knowable.evidence: Filing dates and item codes enumerated from the SEC EDGAR 2022 8-K filing list for CIK 0001836981, verified this session

discriminators: Order/demand quality: are 'pre-orders', 'LOIs' or 'design wins' backed by real deposits and binding terms with identifiable, capacity-matched counterparties — or are they $0-deposit, non-binding indications from shell entities? (Lordstown)

Cash-raise behavior and timing: does management raise equity on a disciplined schedule tied to a capex/hiring plan, or does it exhaust one ATM/PIPE and immediately open a much larger one right as the stock spikes — i.e., is the company a net seller of its own stock into retail mania? (MicroVision)

Diluted share-count trajectory: track shares outstanding filing-to-filing (10-K cover pages, 10-Qs); >25-40% annual growth funding operating losses (not accretive, cash-generative M&A) is a structural tell that shows up in filings months before the price catches down to it (SoundHound)

Revenue-to-market-cap sanity check: a simple, always-available test — does the implied market cap require the company to already be a multiple of its current revenue, with that revenue itself concentrated in a handful of customers (SoundHound: 61-67% from 3 customers) or barely existent (MicroVision: $3.1M revenue)?

Related-party / customer-as-financier structure: are the biggest 'customers' or 'partners' also investors, SPAC sponsors, or paid substantially in the company's own stock — creating revenue that looks real but is circular?

Internal-control and filing-hygiene signals: late 10-Q/10-K filings, Item 4.02 non-reliance/restatement 8-Ks, or an unusual cluster of Item 5.02 executive-departure 8-Ks in a single year are dated, public, and consistently preceded the worst of each collapse in this cohort (Lordstown, BigBear.ai)

Exchange-compliance notices (Item 3.01 8-Ks: NYSE/Nasdaq minimum price or filing-deficiency letters) are the market infrastructure's own dated confirmation that a name has already broken — cheap to monitor and available before most retail investors notice

Cost-cutting disclosures that name 'cash burn' as the reason (Item 2.05 8-Ks / RIF announcements) are management admitting, in writing, that the growth story is behind the burn rate — usually months before the stock fully reprices

Short-seller/investigative reports that make specific, checkable claims (named counterparties, exact dollar figures, verifiable addresses) are far more predictive than reports making only qualitative or valuation-based claims — the checkable ones in this cohort were later substantiated by the company's own board investigation or restatement

Absence of these red flags is itself informative: a pre-profit name with binding contracts backed by deposits, a stable-to-slowly-growing share count, diversified customers, clean filing history, and no exchange-compliance notices is a materially different risk profile from a 'bumper' even when the price chart looks similar — this is the fundamental-analysis floor the task explicitly said isn't sufficient, but its absence is a necessary (not sufficient) warning sign

findings.signal: R&D intensity (R&D/market value), especially in beaten-down 'growth' stocks
findings.effect_size: Qualitative in the source I opened: high-R&D-relative-to-market-value firms 'show strong signs of mis-pricing' and 'subsequently earn large excess returns'; also finds R&D intensity raises return volatility. NBER abstract does not give a precise bps/alpha number — I did not locate the exact long-short spread from an opened source this session (likely stated in the JoF full text, which I could not open, being paywalled).
findings.horizon: Not stated in the abstract I opened; the paper's design uses multi-year (annual, cumulated) return windows on CRSP/Compustat firms
findings.paper: The Stock Market Valuation of Research and Development Expenditures
findings.authors_year: Chan, Lakonishok & Sougiannis (2001), Journal of Finance 56(6)
findings.url_or_doi: https://www.nber.org/papers/w7223 (NBER WP version, opened); DOI 10.1111/0022-1082.00411 (confirmed via CrossRef API, opened)
findings.caveats: Opened the NBER working-paper abstract page and CrossRef metadata directly this session (not a search snippet). Sample is CRSP/Compustat-listed R&D-reporting firms, not micro-cap pre-revenue names specifically. No transaction-cost adjustment mentioned in the abstract; small-cap illiquidity and 1975-1995-era market structure are not addressed there. Being a 2001 paper, any R&D-based mispricing signal is a strong candidate for McLean & Pontiff (2016) publication-decay erosion (see below) since it has been public for 25 years.
findings.applies_to_pre_profit_small_caps: Partial fit: the paper's core claim (market underprices R&D relative to book/market value, esp. in depressed growth stocks) is directionally consistent with a pre-profit small-cap emerging-sector thesis, but the sample skews to larger, longer-listed firms with the accounting/reporting history the paper's R&D-capitalization methodology needs — it does not isolate zero-revenue or IPO-stage names.

findings.signal: Innovative efficiency = patents (or patent citations) per R&D dollar
findings.effect_size: Not independently confirmed this session — the abstract text was withheld by both CrossRef and Semantic Scholar APIs (publisher-restricted), and the Elsevier ScienceDirect/linkinghub pages returned 403/redirect-only content. I confirmed the paper's existence, exact title, authors, year and DOI via CrossRef metadata and the Elsevier linkinghub redirect target, but the specific long-short alpha figure I would otherwise cite is recalled from training knowledge, not from a page I opened this session, so I am not reporting it as verified fact.
findings.horizon: Recalled (unverified this session): 1-year-ahead annual return sorts, updated periodically as new patents are granted with a lag
findings.paper: Innovative Efficiency and Stock Returns
findings.authors_year: Hirshleifer, Hsu & Li (2013), Journal of Financial Economics 107(3)
findings.url_or_doi: DOI 10.1016/j.jfineco.2012.09.011 (confirmed bibliographic record via CrossRef API and Elsevier linkinghub redirect target, both opened this session; full text is paywalled and could not be opened)
findings.caveats: Only bibliographic metadata (title/authors/year/DOI) was verified via an opened page/API this session; the quantitative effect size is NOT verified this session and should be treated as an unconfirmed recollection until the full text or an SSRN/NBER working-paper copy is opened. Innovative-efficiency measures require patent-citation data with multi-year lags, which is a structural problem for very young small-cap issuers that have almost no patent history yet — a first-order caveat for applying this to 'bumper' detection pre-profitability.
findings.applies_to_pre_profit_small_caps: Weak fit as-is: the measure needs several years of patent/R&D history to compute innovative efficiency, which very young pre-revenue issuers (e.g. a 2-year-old quantum-computing IPO) typically lack. Would need adaptation (e.g. patent pace vs. burn rate) to apply pre-profitability.

findings.signal: Stock-market-implied private value of granted patents (scaled innovation-value measure), aggregated to firm level
findings.effect_size: From the CrossRef abstract I opened: the authors' patent-value measure 'correlates with patent citations' and is linked to 'growth, reallocation, and creative destruction'; the paper's headline claim is that technology shocks measured this way 'drive medium-term aggregate economic fluctuations.' This is primarily a measure-construction/macro paper, not a firm-level long-short return-predictability study, so no long-short spread is reported in the abstract.
findings.horizon: Medium-term aggregate fluctuations (business-cycle frequency), not a single-stock trading horizon
findings.paper: Technological Innovation, Resource Allocation, and Growth
findings.authors_year: Kogan, Papanikolaou, Seru & Stoffman (2017), Quarterly Journal of Economics 132(2)
findings.caveats: Opened the OUP article page (confirmed title/existence, full abstract text was JS-gated so I used the CrossRef API record instead, also opened directly) and confirmed via Unpaywall that there is no open-access copy (best_oa_location: null) — full text not independently read this session. The paper's own patent-value dataset (Kogan-Papanikolaou-Seru-Stoffman 'KPSS' patent value data) is the more directly useful artifact for a bumper-detection pipeline than the paper's macro finding — it gives a market-based per-patent dollar value you could compute for a small-cap's patent portfolio.
findings.applies_to_pre_profit_small_caps: Indirectly useful: the KPSS patent-value construction (event-study stock reaction on patent grant day) can in principle be computed for any listed firm with patents, including pre-profit ones, making it more usable for bumper detection than efficiency ratios that need years of R&D history — but the paper itself studies aggregate growth dynamics, not a stock-picking signal for small caps.

findings.signal: Organization capital (SG&A-capitalized measure of firm-specific human/organizational capital)
findings.effect_size: From the CrossRef abstract I opened directly: firms with higher organization capital 'exhibit greater shareholder risk and average returns 4.6% higher than those with lower capital' (i.e., roughly a 4.6-percentage-point annual return spread, high-minus-low organization capital, consistent with a risk-based - not pure-mispricing - explanation in the paper's framing).
findings.horizon: Annual return spread (long-short, sorted on organization-capital-to-total-capital ratio)
findings.paper: Organization Capital and the Cross-Section of Expected Returns
findings.caveats: Verified via CrossRef API metadata/abstract opened directly this session; the Wiley/Online Library full-text page returned 403 (paywalled, not opened) and the NBER working-paper mirror I tried (guessed number w17138) turned out to be an unrelated Denmark disability-pension paper, so I could not cross-check the 4.6% figure against a second opened source. Organization capital (built from cumulated, depreciated SG&A) is essentially undefined or noisy for firms with very short operating histories and low/no SG&A base — a structural mismatch for pre-revenue small caps.
findings.applies_to_pre_profit_small_caps: Weak fit: the SG&A-capitalization methodology needs several years of income-statement history to build a meaningful organization-capital stock; very young, pre-profit issuers (limited SG&A history, often R&D-heavy rather than SG&A-heavy) are close to the edge case this measure was not built for.

findings.signal: Patent/citation productivity surprises relative to R&D spending (innovation output vs. R&D input mismatch)
findings.effect_size: Not independently confirmed this session — CrossRef, Semantic Scholar, and the OUP article-lookup page all withheld the abstract text (paywalled/JS-gated); I confirmed the paper's exact title ('Misvaluing Innovation'), authors, year, journal, volume/issue and page range (RFS 26(3), pp. 635-666) directly from the OUP page and CrossRef, but the specific abnormal-return figure I would cite is recalled from training knowledge, not confirmed against an opened source this session.
findings.horizon: Recalled (unverified this session): annual, sorted on patent-and-citation counts scaled by R&D, holding for roughly a year following the innovation-output measurement
findings.paper: Misvaluing Innovation
findings.authors_year: Cohen, Diether & Malloy (2013), Review of Financial Studies 26(3)
findings.caveats: Only bibliographic identity was verified via an opened page this session; the quantitative long-short spread is NOT verified this session. The 'innovation output surprise' construct needs a firm to already be filing/being granted patents at meaningful volume, which limits applicability to very early-stage, patent-thin small caps.
findings.applies_to_pre_profit_small_caps: Similar limitation to Hirshleifer-Hsu-Li: needs patent history to compute the surprise term, which a genuinely pre-revenue/early-stage bumper candidate may not yet have.

findings.signal: Meta-finding: out-of-sample and post-publication decay of published return-predictor spreads (applies to every signal above)
findings.effect_size: Quoted directly from the CrossRef abstract I opened: across 97 published return-predicting variables, 'portfolio returns are 26% lower out-of-sample and 58% lower post-publication,' with an estimated 32-percentage-point incremental decline attributable to publication-informed trading; decay is larger for predictors that had higher in-sample returns and is concentrated in less liquid, high-idiosyncratic-risk stocks.
findings.horizon: Out-of-sample (pre-publication but post-original-sample) vs. post-publication, evaluated across the full post-publication history of each predictor
findings.paper: Does Academic Research Destroy Stock Return Predictability?
findings.caveats: Verified via CrossRef API abstract, opened directly this session, with the quoted numbers matching my prior training knowledge of this well-known paper — this is the strongest-confidence finding in this sweep.
findings.applies_to_pre_profit_small_caps: Directly relevant to every innovation/R&D signal above rather than to a specific stock cohort: all four academic papers (CLS 2001, HHL 2013, EP 2013, CDM 2013) are now 12-25 years old and have been public long enough that, per this paper's own finding, their documented spreads should be expected to have decayed toward roughly 40-75% of their original in-sample magnitude, and the effect is worst precisely in the illiquid, high-idiosyncratic-risk small-cap names this task cares about — meaning any of these signals used mechanically today on pre-profit small caps should be assumed weaker than the original papers report, not stronger.

base_rates: SPAC post-merger returns (verified via a Wikipedia summary page I opened directly this session, which itself cites the underlying academic studies rather than being read from the primary papers): for U.S. SPACs merging Dec 2012-Jun 2021, average post-merger-announcement stock price declines of -14.1% at 1 year and -18% at 2 years; a separate Dec-2022 analysis found SPACs that completed mergers between Jul 2020-Dec 2021 (the boom vintage) had fallen 'over 60% from the standard $10 per share' and underperformed traditional IPOs by 26% over the same window. I did NOT independently open the primary sources (Klausner/Ohlrogge/Ruan 'A Sober Look at SPACs', or Gahng/Ritter/Zhang) this session — flag this as a secondary-source confirmation, not a primary-source read, and note the SPAC boom-vintage figure is dominated by 2020-2021, a single unusually distorted episode.

IPO long-run underperformance (partially verified): Jay Ritter's IPO data site (opened directly this session) confirms it maintains a 'long-run returns' dataset for U.S. IPOs, but I could not retrieve the specific document (a direct-link guess 404'd) to quote an exact 3-year buy-and-hold figure this session. The commonly cited finding from this literature (Ritter 1991; Ritter & Welch 2002) — roughly 20-30% average 3-year underperformance of IPO cohorts relative to size/book-to-market-matched non-issuers, with very wide dispersion and the worst underperformance concentrated in small, high-turnover, non-profitable issuers — is recalled from training knowledge and was NOT re-confirmed against an opened primary source this session; treat as an unverified prior pending a follow-up read of Ritter's actual dataset.

Fraction of loss-making/pre-profit small caps that beat the market over 3-5 years: I could not locate and open a specific primary source giving this exact base rate within this session's tool budget (WebSearch was already exhausted at the start of this task — see note below — and targeted WebFetch guesses at Ritter/NBER/SSRN URLs for this specific stat did not resolve). This is a genuine gap, not a number I'm willing to assert; the closest adjacent, actually-verified fact is McLean & Pontiff's general finding that predictor-based excess returns decay sharply out of sample and post-publication, which should bias any 'edge' estimate for this cohort downward. Recommend a dedicated follow-up using CRSP/Compustat cut by profitability decile (e.g. via the Fama-French/Ken French data library's profitability-sorted portfolios, or a screen of Compustat firms with negative trailing-12-month net income) before treating any number here as fact.

IMPORTANT SESSION CONSTRAINT: the WebSearch tool reported its quota already exhausted (200/200 calls used) on the very first search I issued in this task, before I had used any myself — so essentially this entire literature sweep was done via direct WebFetch calls to DOI redirects, the CrossRef and Semantic Scholar APIs, NBER/OUP/Elsevier pages, and Unpaywall, never via a general web search. That materially constrained my ability to locate SSRN/NBER working-paper mirrors with full abstracts (several attempts 404'd or hit CAPTCHA walls on DuckDuckGo/Bing). Flagging this so the orchestrator knows the search-engine layer, not just the target papers, was the limiting factor.

findings.signal: MAX effect — maximum daily return over trailing month (proxy for lottery/skewness demand)
findings.effect_size: Value-weighted return spread between lowest- and highest-MAX deciles exceeds 1% per month (after controlling for size, book-to-market, momentum, short-term reversal, and illiquidity); including MAX also subsumes/reverses the idiosyncratic-volatility discount.
findings.horizon: 1-month portfolio formation/holding, tested over the paper's full sample (US stocks, ~1962-2005)
findings.paper: Maxing Out: Stocks as Lotteries and the Cross-Section of Expected Returns
findings.url_or_doi: Journal of Financial Economics, Vol. 99, Issue 2, pp. 427-446 (verified via https://ideas.repec.org/a/eee/jfinec/v99y2011i2p427-446.html)
findings.caveats: Effect is a monthly cross-sectional spread from decile sorts, not a guaranteed path for any single name; sample predates the 2020-2021 SPAC/meme-stock retail-options era that arguably intensified lottery demand (a plausible post-sample regime shift, unverified this session); small/illiquid stocks drive much of the MAX decile spread, so transaction costs likely eat a large share; McLean & Pontiff (2016, below) find anomaly returns shrink materially post-publication.
findings.applies_to_pre_profit_small_caps: Directly on-point as a base rate against 'high-optionality, high-single-stock-volatility' pre-profit names: it says the segment of the market with the highest lottery-like payoff draws (large positive skew, big single-day spikes) has, on average, LOWER subsequent returns, not higher — the opposite of the 'next NVDA/Nebius' framing. It does not say no individual name in that bucket wins big; it says the bucket as a whole is overpriced for the lottery ticket.

findings.signal: Retail/gambling-propensity demand for lottery-type stocks (low price, high idiosyncratic volatility/skewness)
findings.effect_size: Lottery-type stocks subsequently underperform; the socioeconomic clienteles that buy state lottery tickets are the same ones concentrated in lottery-stock holdings, and poorer/less-diversified investors bear disproportionate losses from this tilt.
findings.horizon: Cross-sectional, multi-year holding-period underperformance (US retail brokerage data, 1991-1996 primary sample)
findings.paper: Who Gambles in the Stock Market?
findings.url_or_doi: Journal of Finance, Vol. 64, Issue 4, pp. 1889-1933 (verified via https://ideas.repec.org/a/bla/jfinan/v64y2009i4p1889-1933.html)
findings.caveats: Sample is a single discount brokerage's retail clients from the 1990s — a very different market microstructure than today's zero-commission, options-heavy, social-media-amplified retail flow; the paper documents WHO buys these stocks and that they underperform, but is not itself a clean asset-pricing test with a published alpha figure I could extract from the abstract alone.
findings.applies_to_pre_profit_small_caps: Relevant as a base rate on WHY narrative-driven, low-priced, pre-profit small caps get bid up beyond fundamentals (gambling-motivated retail demand) even though the average outcome is underperformance — useful context for a 'bumper' screen that must distinguish genuine informed accumulation from lottery-demand froth.

findings.signal: Idiosyncratic volatility (high trailing idiosyncratic vol relative to Fama-French 3-factor model)
findings.effect_size: Stocks with high idiosyncratic volatility earn 'abysmally low' average returns not explained by market, size, value, or momentum exposures; the paper reports this as a puzzle relative to standard risk-based pricing (qualitative confirmation of a strong negative spread; I could not pull the exact percentage-per-month figure from the abstract text alone this session).
findings.horizon: Monthly rebalanced portfolios, US sample 1963-2000
findings.paper: The Cross-Section of Volatility and Expected Returns
findings.url_or_doi: Journal of Finance, Vol. 61, Issue 1, pp. 259-299 (verified via https://ideas.repec.org/a/bla/jfinan/v61y2006i1p259-299.html and cross-checked on Wikipedia's Low-volatility anomaly page)
findings.caveats: Effect size number not independently pulled from primary text this session (only abstract-level synthesis via RePEc/Wikipedia, not the full PDF) — treat magnitude as inferred, not verified; later literature (e.g., Fu 2009, Huang et al. 2010) debated whether this is a real risk premium or largely a short-term reversal/liquidity artifact — that debate was not itself checked this session.
findings.applies_to_pre_profit_small_caps: Directly applicable: pre-profit small caps in an unproven sector are close to the textbook definition of 'high idiosyncratic volatility' names. The base rate this establishes is that the average payoff to holding the single most volatile slice of the market has historically been poor, not good — a screen built on volatility/optionality alone is fighting a documented anomaly, not exploiting one.

findings.signal: Value vs. glamour (extrapolation of past growth into high valuation multiples)
findings.effect_size: Contrarian (low-multiple/'value') strategies outperform glamour strategies; the paper attributes this to investors extrapolating past growth and overpaying for glamour/growth names, not to glamour stocks being fundamentally riskier.
findings.horizon: 5-year holding-period returns, US sample 1968-1990 (NYSE/AMEX)
findings.paper: Contrarian Investment, Extrapolation, and Risk
findings.url_or_doi: Journal of Finance, Vol. 49, Issue 5, pp. 1541-1578 (verified via https://ideas.repec.org/a/bla/jfinan/v49y1994i5p1541-78.html)
findings.caveats: Sample ends 1990, well before the multi-decade growth-stock outperformance of 1995-2021 in the US, so 'value beats glamour' is itself a base rate that has had long multi-year periods of failing badly (publication-decay/regime-dependence concern, consistent with McLean & Pontiff below); pre-profit sector-emergence stocks are a specific subtype of glamour (extreme growth expectation, not just high multiple) that the original LSV sample was not built to isolate.
findings.applies_to_pre_profit_small_caps: The mechanism (extrapolative overpricing of exciting growth narratives) is exactly the risk in a 'bumper' thesis: the base rate says the average high-extrapolation glamour name has disappointed relative to its price, which is the null hypothesis a bumper-detection process needs to beat, not assume away.

findings.signal: Anomaly concentration by firm size (asset-growth and other anomalies present in micro/small caps, largely absent in large caps)
findings.effect_size: Several return anomalies (net stock issues, accruals, momentum) appear across all size groups, but the asset-growth anomaly specifically is present in microcap and small stocks and absent in big stocks — i.e., mispricing-consistent patterns are stronger where limits to arbitrage (short-sale costs, liquidity) are worse.
findings.horizon: Monthly cross-sectional portfolio sorts, US sample through mid-2000s
findings.paper: Dissecting Anomalies
findings.url_or_doi: Journal of Finance, Vol. 63, Issue 4, pp. 1653-1678 (verified via https://ideas.repec.org/a/bla/jfinan/v63y2008i4p1653-1678.html)
findings.caveats: This is the Fama-French paper most directly about WHERE anomalies concentrate by size, not the original 1992/1993 factor papers; effect sizes for the specific anomaly-by-size breakdown were not independently pulled from the primary tables this session, only the qualitative abstract-level finding.
findings.applies_to_pre_profit_small_caps: Establishes the general base rate that small/micro-cap mispricing is both larger AND harder to arbitrage away — cuts both ways for a bumper screen: genuine informational edges plausibly persist longer in this segment, but so do behavioral overpricing errors (glamour, lottery demand) documented above.

findings.signal: Long-run IPO underperformance, especially unprofitable issuers
findings.effect_size: 1980-2024, unprofitable IPO issuers (n=3,926): average 3-year buy-and-hold return -0.5% raw / -30.7% market-adjusted / -23.4% style-adjusted (vs. profitable issuers at +33.6%/-13.0%/+1.8%). Full 1980-2024 sample (9,253 IPOs) averages -20.5% market-adjusted / -8.9% style-adjusted over 3 years. Distribution (1975-2021, n=9,195): 38.5% of IPOs had a 3-year buy-and-hold return below -50% (measured from first close); only ~15.7% exceeded +100% and only ~1.7% exceeded +500% over 3 years.
findings.horizon: 3-year and 5-year buy-and-hold from first closing price, updated through Dec 2025
findings.paper: Initial Public Offerings: Updated Long-run Statistics (living dataset; academic root is Ritter & Welch, 'A Review of IPO Activity, Pricing, and Allocations,' Journal of Finance, 2002)
findings.authors_year: Ritter (updated Aug 27, 2026 edition, tables through Feb-Jul 2026)
findings.caveats: This is Ritter's continuously-updated working dataset, not a single peer-reviewed snapshot — treat table dates (e.g. 'Table 16b updated February 16, 2026') as the retrieval-relevant vintage; returns for recent cohorts (2023-2024) are measured over incomplete/short windows; style/market-adjustment methodology choices (CRSP value-weighted index, book-to-market-matched control firms) affect magnitudes; excludes sub-$5 penny-stock IPOs from the main tables (a separate table shows those perform even worse: -52.4% market-adjusted 3-year return for 2001-2024 sub-$8 file-price-range IPOs).
findings.applies_to_pre_profit_small_caps: This is the single most directly applicable base rate in the sweep: it isolates exactly the 'unprofitable, recently-public, small' cohort the user wants a bumper detector for, and the answer is that on average this cohort loses ~20-30 percentage points against a matched benchmark over 3 years, with a fat left tail (over a third lose more than half their value) and a thin right tail (under 2% deliver 500%+ style 'bumper' outcomes).

findings.signal: deSPAC (post-merger SPAC) returns
findings.effect_size: 447 business combinations, 2010-2022: average 3-year buy-and-hold return -57.7% (market return over same holding periods averaged +17.0%), i.e. -74.7% market-adjusted on average. By merger-year cohort, 3-year market-adjusted returns are negative in nearly every year (e.g. 2020 cohort: -84.6%; 2021 cohort: -80.0%; 2022 cohort: -80.7%).
findings.horizon: 1-year and 3-year buy-and-hold post-merger, updated through 2025
findings.paper: Updated version of Table 4 in 'SPACs' (Gahng, Ritter & Zhang, Review of Financial Studies, Sept. 2023), reproduced in Ritter's live long-run-returns document
findings.authors_year: Gahng, Ritter & Zhang (2023); table updated by Ritter through July 2026
findings.url_or_doi: https://site.warrington.ufl.edu/ritter/files/IPOs-long-run-returns-on-IPOs.pdf, Table 15c (fetched and read directly this session)
findings.caveats: SPACResearch.com is the primary underlying data source (secondary, not independently re-derived from raw filings this session); returns depend heavily on redemption-rate assumptions and side-payment structures the table itself flags as complicating comparability across deSPACs; 2023-2025 figures use an assumed $10 entry price rather than actual first-close price, a methodology change from earlier years.
findings.applies_to_pre_profit_small_caps: SPAC mergers are one of the main historical vehicles that took pre-profit, early-stage, story-driven small caps (EV, space, some AI/robotics names) public; the near-universal negative multi-year market-adjusted return across merger-year cohorts is a strong prior against 'a SPAC-merged pre-profit small cap is likely to be the next big winner.'

findings.signal: SPAC structural dilution (trust value per share erodes well before any merger)
findings.effect_size: Mean net cash per share fell from the nominal $10.00 raised to a mean of $4.10 (median $5.70) for SPACs merging Jan 2019-Jun 2020; somewhat higher but still well below $10 for the Jun 2020-Nov 2021 cohort. The paper characterizes these costs as 'higher than has been previously recognized, and higher than the cost of an IPO,' concentrated on shareholders who hold through the merger while sponsors gain disproportionately.
findings.horizon: From SPAC IPO through de-SPAC merger date (typically 1-2 years)
findings.paper: A Sober Look at SPACs
findings.url_or_doi: Yale Journal on Regulation, Vol. 39, Issue 1 (verified via https://www.yalejreg.com/print/a-sober-look-at-spacs/)
findings.caveats: Published in a law/policy journal rather than a peer-reviewed finance journal, so it did not go through the same referee process as the other papers here; sample period (2019-2021) captures the SPAC boom/bust, plausibly the worst-case window for this structure rather than a representative one; law-and-economics framing emphasizes structural/mechanical costs (redemption dynamics, warrant dilution) rather than a return-predictability regression.
findings.applies_to_pre_profit_small_caps: Mechanically explains part of why deSPAC pre-profit small caps underperform on average (above): a meaningful share of the loss is structural dilution baked in before the operating story even starts trading, independent of whether the underlying business turns out to be a genuine 'bumper.'

findings.signal: Publication decay of documented return-predictability signals
findings.effect_size: Directionally, the paper finds that anomaly/predictor returns shrink substantially after academic publication (post-publication decay), consistent with markets partially learning about and arbitraging away documented signals; I could not extract the specific percentage decay figure from the abstract-level fetch this session.
findings.horizon: Pre- vs. post-publication comparison across dozens of published return-predictor variables, US sample
findings.paper: Does Academic Research Destroy Stock Return Predictability?
findings.url_or_doi: Journal of Finance, Vol. 71, Issue 1, pp. 5-32 (verified via https://ideas.repec.org/a/bla/jfinan/v71y2016i1p5-32.html)
findings.caveats: Effect-size figure (commonly cited elsewhere as roughly a 35-58% decline in a signal's return post-publication, and closer to 100% for a subset after including out-of-sample and post-publication periods together) is widely quoted in secondary sources but was NOT independently verified from primary text this session — flag as inferred/unverified, not confirmed.
findings.applies_to_pre_profit_small_caps: This is the key caveat for every OTHER finding in this sweep: MAX, idiosyncratic-vol, and value/glamour effects are all long-published (1994-2013); to the extent markets have partially arbitraged them since publication, their historical effect sizes are upper bounds on what a bumper-screen built purely on these signals should expect going forward.

base_rates: Unprofitable IPO issuers, 1980-2024 (n=3,926, Ritter dataset, verified 2026-09-25): average 3-year buy-and-hold return -0.5% raw, -30.7% market-adjusted, -23.4% style-adjusted vs. matched non-issuers — i.e., on average this cohort loses roughly a quarter of relative value over 3 years.

All IPOs 1975-2021 (n=9,195, Ritter dataset): 38.5% had a 3-year buy-and-hold return below -50% (measured from first close); only about 15.7% exceeded +100%; only about 1.7% exceeded +500% — the 'bumper' outcome (multi-bagger) is a thin right tail, not the median case, even before conditioning on profitability.

deSPAC mergers 2010-2022 (n=447, Gahng/Ritter/Zhang dataset updated through 2026): average 3-year buy-and-hold return -57.7% raw, -74.7% market-adjusted — nearly every merger-year cohort from 2012-2022 underperformed the market over the following 3 years.

SPAC structural dilution: mean net trust cash per share fell from a nominal $10.00 to $4.10 (2019-mid-2020 cohort) before any merger-specific business risk even begins (Klausner, Ohlrogge & Ruan 2022) — a mechanical headwind layered on top of business risk for any SPAC-merged pre-profit small cap.

MAX-effect decile spread (Bali, Cakici & Whitelaw 2011): stocks in the highest 'lottery-like maximum daily return' decile underperform the lowest decile by over 1%/month on a risk-adjusted basis — i.e., the segment of the market that looks most like a 'bumper' by raw payoff-shape (huge daily spikes, high skew) has, on average, delivered the worst forward returns, not the best.

Idiosyncratic volatility puzzle (Ang, Hodrick, Xing & Zhang 2006): stocks with the highest trailing idiosyncratic volatility relative to the Fama-French 3-factor model earn abnormally low subsequent average returns not explained by standard risk factors — again, the 'most volatile/optionality-rich' bucket underperforms on average.

General small-cap/micro-cap anomaly base rate (Fama & French 2008): documented mispricing-consistent anomalies (e.g., asset growth) concentrate specifically in microcap and small stocks and are largely absent in large caps, consistent with weaker arbitrage forces there — this cuts both ways (genuine edges may persist longer, but so do behavioral overpricing errors like the glamour/lottery effects above).

Publication/arbitrage decay (McLean & Pontiff 2016, directionally verified, magnitude not independently confirmed this session): published return-predictor effect sizes shrink materially once documented in the academic literature — meaning the historical spreads quoted above (MAX effect, idiosyncratic vol, value-glamour) are plausible upper bounds on what a screen built on the same signals should expect prospectively, decades after original publication.

Synthesis / net base rate for a 'pre-profit, sector-not-yet-profitable, high-optionality small cap' bucket: every base rate located and opened this session points the same direction — average forward risk-adjusted returns for this bucket are negative to flat, the loss distribution is fat-tailed on the downside, and true multi-bagger 'bumper' outcomes are a small minority of the bucket, not the modal outcome. This does not mean no individual name succeeds (NVDA-2020, Nebius-type outcomes clearly exist ex post) — it means picking the eventual winner out of the bucket, rather than owning the bucket, is exactly the hard problem the literature says fundamentals-only or volatility/skew-based screens have not been shown to solve; it supports the user's own instinct that a fundamentals-only screen is necessary-but-not-sufficient and that a separate, higher-order signal-detection or judge layer is where the edge (if any) would have to come from.

findings.signal: Opportunistic (non-routine) insider purchases — especially by local, non-executive insiders at weakly-governed firms
findings.effect_size: Value-weighted long-short 'opportunistic insider' portfolio earns ~82 bps/month abnormal return; 'routine' insider trades (predictable, repeated pattern) earn ~0 abnormal return
findings.horizon: Monthly-rebalanced signal; alpha accrues over following ~12 months
findings.paper: Decoding Inside Information
findings.authors_year: Cohen, Malloy & Pomorski (2012), Journal of Finance 67(3)
findings.caveats: 1986-2011 Form-4 sample. Classifying a trade as 'routine' vs 'opportunistic' requires 3+ years of that insider's trading history — mechanically unusable for a company in its first ~3 years public, which is exactly the bumper-detection window. Opportunistic insiders draw more SEC scrutiny post-detection (noted in-paper), and McLean-Pontiff decay applies since this is a well-cited, 13-year-old published result.
findings.applies_to_pre_profit_small_caps: Weak in the first 1-3 years post-listing (no trading history to classify routine vs opportunistic); more applicable once a name has 3+ years of insider Form-4 history.

findings.signal: Insider purchase intensity (sells are largely uninformative)
findings.effect_size: Insider purchases predict positive future cross-sectional returns and are strongest in smaller firms; insider sales show little predictive power. Precise long-short spread not independently re-derived beyond the abstract this session.
findings.horizon: ~12 months following filing
findings.paper: Are Insider Trades Informative?
findings.authors_year: Lakonishok & Lee (2001), Review of Financial Studies 14(1)
findings.caveats: 1975-1995 sample — pre-Reg FD, pre-decimalization; small-firm result could partly reflect liquidity/microstructure rather than pure information content. No modern (post-2000) out-of-sample re-test opened this session.
findings.applies_to_pre_profit_small_caps: Moderate — one of the few papers to explicitly document a stronger signal in smaller firms, but the 1975-1995 'small firm' distribution is not the same population as a 2020s pre-revenue quantum/robotics micro-cap.

findings.signal: Change in breadth of mutual-fund/institutional ownership
findings.effect_size: Stocks in the lowest decile of prior-quarter breadth CHANGE underperform the highest-decile stocks by 6.38% over the next 12 months (4.95% after standard factor adjustment)
findings.horizon: 12 months
findings.paper: Breadth of Ownership and Stock Returns
findings.authors_year: Chen, Hong & Stein (2002), Journal of Financial Economics 66(2-3)
findings.caveats: Uses 1979-1998 mutual fund holdings (quarterly, reported with a lag, 13F-adjacent). Mechanism is short-sale-constraint/disagreement driven: narrow ownership signals binding short-sale constraints and OVERvaluation, i.e. this is a sell/avoid signal for low-breadth names, not a buy signal.
findings.applies_to_pre_profit_small_caps: Inverted relevance — a genuinely early-stage 'bumper' in an unprofitable emerging sector is almost by definition low-breadth (few generalist funds hold it yet), which this model reads as a negative signal. The usable transfer is watching breadth RISE over time (institutional discovery), not the static low level.

findings.signal: Low short interest among heavily-traded stocks
findings.effect_size: Low-short-interest, heavily-traded stocks show statistically and economically significant positive abnormal returns, larger in magnitude than the (temporary, marginal) negative return to high-short-interest names
findings.horizon: Not re-derived beyond abstract this session (short-interest literature typically uses 1-6 month post-formation windows)
findings.paper: The Good News in Short Interest
findings.authors_year: Boehmer, Huszar & Jordan (2010), Journal of Financial Economics 96(1)
findings.caveats: Sample explicitly restricted to 'heavily traded' stocks, which by construction excludes the thin-float micro-caps a bumper search would target.
findings.applies_to_pre_profit_small_caps: Low — the paper's own liquidity screen excludes the target universe, and short interest data is often unavailable or unreliable (hard-to-borrow, no listed options) for genuine micro-caps.

findings.signal: Aggregate (market-wide) short interest
findings.effect_size: Predicts AGGREGATE market returns with in- and out-of-sample R² ≈ 13% annually; utility gains to a mean-variance investor >300 bps/year from using the signal, operating mainly through a cash-flow forecasting channel
findings.horizon: Annual
findings.paper: Short Interest and Aggregate Stock Returns
findings.authors_year: Rapach, Ringgenberg & Zhou (2016), Journal of Financial Economics 121(1)
findings.caveats: This is a market-timing signal, not a stock-picking signal.
findings.applies_to_pre_profit_small_caps: Not applicable at the single-stock level — it is a macro overlay at best (e.g., caution on small-cap beta broadly when aggregate short interest is elevated), not a bumper-identification tool.

findings.signal: Sell-side analyst buy/sell recommendation changes
findings.effect_size: New buy recommendations show a modest positive drift; new sell/drop recommendations show a materially larger negative drift (roughly -9% over 6 months per the abstract synthesis) — the buy-side split of the exact stated number was not independently re-derived from the primary text this session, only from a secondary abstract summary, so treat the precise split as inferred rather than fully confirmed.
findings.horizon: Up to 6 months; the negative (sell) signal is stronger and more persistent than the positive (buy) signal
findings.paper: Do Brokerage Analysts' Recommendations Have Investment Value?
findings.caveats: 1989-1991 sample from large investment banks, predates the 2003 Global Settlement/Reg AC analyst-conflict reforms that changed how recommendations are distributed (far fewer 'sell' ratings issued today, which mechanically weakens the historical asymmetry going forward).
findings.applies_to_pre_profit_small_caps: Plausible but not directly tested here — pre-profit small caps in a nascent sector typically carry 0-1 analysts, so the coverage-INITIATION event itself (not the direction of the first rating) is arguably the more relevant bumper signal; that specific effect was not verified from a paper opened this session.

findings.signal: 13F hedge-fund equity holdings vs. mutual-fund holdings ('smart money' stock-picking skill)
findings.effect_size: COULD NOT VERIFY THIS SESSION. Every route to the abstract or PDF (Wiley/RFS, faculty page, SSRN) returned 403/404. Only bibliographic metadata (title, authors, journal, year, DOI) confirmed via Crossref and Semantic Scholar cross-check. Do not treat any specific alpha figure for this paper as verified.
findings.horizon: Unverified
findings.paper: How Smart Are the Smart Guys? A Unique View from Hedge Fund Stock Holdings
findings.authors_year: Griffin & Xu (2009), Review of Financial Studies 22(7)
findings.caveats: Flagging per epistemic-honesty rule rather than reporting a number from training-data recall. Existence and venue confirmed; content not opened.
findings.applies_to_pre_profit_small_caps: Unknown — not verified this session.

findings.signal: Fund managers' single highest-conviction ('best idea') 13F position, inferred from position sizing relative to a manager's own portfolio
findings.effect_size: COULD NOT VERIFY THIS SESSION. SSRN abstract page blocked/404 on every fetch attempt; only title/authors/DOI confirmed via Crossref. Any specific alpha number commonly cited for this paper is training-data recall, NOT verified — explicitly not reported here.
findings.horizon: Unverified
findings.paper: Best Ideas
findings.authors_year: Cohen, Polk & Silli (SSRN working paper, first posted ~2005/2009 draft)
findings.caveats: Long-running, widely-cited SSRN working paper; I could not confirm whether/where it was ultimately published in a peer-reviewed journal this session. This is exactly the category the task's evidence bar is meant to filter — treat as unverified until a primary page is actually opened.
findings.applies_to_pre_profit_small_caps: Unknown — not verified this session.

findings.signal: Hedge fund 'crowding' — multiple funds independently buying the same stock in the same quarter
findings.effect_size: Hedge fund equity portfolios are found to be 'remarkably independent' overall; on the occasions crowding does occur it is associated with POSITIVE subsequent returns, and the paper finds no evidence crowded demand destabilizes prices, even in stress periods. Precise bps figure not surfaced in the retrieved abstract.
findings.horizon: Not specified in retrieved abstract
findings.paper: Hedge Fund Crowds and Mispricing
findings.caveats: Directly contradicts the popular 'crowded trade = coming unwind' narrative — worth noting since a bumper thesis often implicitly assumes 'get in before the crowd.' 13F data lags real-time by up to 45 days and only captures long-equity managers with >$100m AUM, under-sampling the smallest/most illiquid names.
findings.applies_to_pre_profit_small_caps: Unclear — the paper's small-cap representation was not checked this session, and 13F's size/lag limitations bite hardest on the pre-profit micro-cap universe.

findings.signal: META-FINDING (applies to every signal above): post-publication decay of academic return predictors
findings.effect_size: Across 97 published cross-sectional return predictors: average portfolio returns are 26% lower out-of-sample (same country, pre-publication) and 58% lower post-publication than in the original in-sample results; ~32% of the post-publication decline is attributed to publication-informed trading (capital chasing the anomaly). Decay is worse for predictors with the strongest original returns; returns hold up somewhat better in high-idiosyncratic-risk, low-liquidity stocks where arbitrage capital struggles to chase the anomaly.
findings.horizon: Cross-sectional, measured from original publication to present
findings.paper: Does Academic Research Destroy Stock Return Predictability?
findings.caveats: Every insider/short-interest/analyst/ownership-breadth paper above is 10-25 years old and has been publicly cited for over a decade — their headline in-sample effect sizes should be treated as upper bounds on what remains tradeable today, not current expectations.
findings.applies_to_pre_profit_small_caps: Actually the most directly relevant and mildly favorable point in this whole sweep: the paper's own finding is that anomalies concentrated in illiquid, high-idiosyncratic-risk stocks (a reasonable description of pre-profit small caps in an emerging sector) resist arbitrage-driven decay better than large-cap-friendly anomalies — but this is inference from one line of the abstract, not a direct test of the target universe, and should be weighted accordingly.

base_rates: Lifetime, most individual US common stocks (CRSP, 1926-2016) underperformed 1-month Treasury bills; the best-performing 4% of listed companies account for the ENTIRE net wealth creation of the US stock market since 1926, with the rest collectively roughly matching T-bills. Positive skewness (a few huge winners) drives this — the 'bumper' hunt is explicitly a search for that top few percent, not a typical outcome. Source: Bessembinder (2018), Journal of Financial Economics 129(3):440-457 — abstract opened via Semantic Scholar API this session.

IPOs broadly (9,253 US operating-company IPOs, 1980-2024, opened directly from Jay Ritter's updated tables, University of Florida, dated Aug 27 2026): average 3-year buy-and-hold return from first closing price = +19.1% raw, but -20.5% market-adjusted and -8.9% style-adjusted vs. matched non-issuers — i.e. the average IPO underperforms a size/book-to-market-matched benchmark over 3 years.

Unprofitable-at-IPO subset specifically (n=3,926 of the above 9,253, 1980-2024): average 3-year buy-and-hold return -0.5% raw, -30.7% market-adjusted, -23.4% style-adjusted — pre-profit issuers underperform noticeably MORE than the full IPO sample on average. Narrower subset (unprofitable, trailing sales <$100m, n=2,880): -10.3% raw, -40.9% market-adjusted.

Distribution of individual IPO outcomes (9,195 IPOs, 1975-2021, opened this session): 38.5% had a 3-year buy-and-hold return worse than -50% (measured from first close); median 3-year BHR was -25.7%. Only about 7.7% had a 3-year return above +200%, and roughly 1.7% above +500% — the right-tail 'bumper' outcome is a small minority even within a sample that already survived to have 3 years of trading.

Unprofitable, small-sales, TECH-specifically issuers (n=789, ex-dot-com-bubble years, 1980-2023): average 3-year buy-and-hold return from first close = +28.4% raw but -19.2% market-adjusted — i.e., this narrowest proxy for a 'pre-profit small-cap tech bumper' still underperforms the market on average despite a positive raw return, though it clearly outperforms the equivalent unprofitable NON-tech small-sales bucket (-7.7% raw, -48.8% market-adjusted, n=1,499).

SPAC mergers (deSPACs) specifically underperform even regular IPOs: 451 deSPAC mergers 2012-2022, average 3-year post-merger buy-and-hold return -57.7% (-74.7% market-adjusted). Separately, SPACs raise $10/share at IPO but the merged company retains on average only about $4.10-$5.70/share of that after sponsor promote and redemption-related dilution, before any operating outcome is even considered. Sources: Ritter's Table 15c (deSPAC returns, updated July 2026, opened this session) and Klausner, Ohlrogge & Ruan (2020) 'A Sober Look at SPACs' (abstract opened via Crossref this session).

IPOs underperform size-matched non-issuing firms by an average of ~3.6%/year (equally weighted) over the first five years post-issue, excluding the first-day pop; ~2.1%/year underperformance vs. size-AND-book-to-market-matched firms. Source: Ritter's Table 20, opened this session.

findings.signal: Google search volume (retail investor attention proxy)
findings.effect_size: Abstract (Crossref, opened this session): high-SVI IPOs show larger first-day pops but subsequent long-run underperformance; momentum is stronger among high-SVI names. Secondary/Scholar-summarized (NOT independently confirmed from primary text this session, publisher paywalled): stocks with the largest SVI increases show positive abnormal price pressure over ~2 weeks that reverses within the year.
findings.horizon: Attention spike -> ~2-week price pressure -> reversal within ~1 year (secondary-source figure, see caveat); IPO effect measured at first-day and long-run (multi-year).
findings.paper: In Search of Attention
findings.caveats: Opened via Crossref abstract API and RePEc/IDEAS citation page (confirms JoF 66(5):1461-1499, 2011; sample = Russell 3000, 2004-2008). Publisher full text (Wiley) returned HTTP 403 to WebFetch and SSRN was blocked by Cloudflare bot-check, so the specific '2-week pop / 1-year reversal' figure could not be re-verified from the primary text this session -- it is carried from a Google-Scholar-rendered summary, so treat that specific number as inferred, not verified. The core abstract claim (SVI predicts IPO first-day pop + long-run underperformance, stronger momentum among high-SVI stocks) IS verified from the actual abstract text. Published 2011, sample ends 2008 -- 18 years of decay exposure (McLean & Pontiff 2016) and the signal (Google Trends) is now a widely-used, crowded quant input.
findings.applies_to_pre_profit_small_caps: Directly on point: this is literally an IPO/attention study. It says attention chasing inflates the pop and is followed by underperformance -- i.e. rising Google search interest in a name is a hype marker, not a fundamentals-free green light. Useful as one input to flag 'the crowd has noticed this bumper candidate' but the paper itself argues that's a fade risk, not a buy signal, on its own.

findings.signal: Media sentiment / pessimism factor (aggregate market-level, from WSJ column text)
findings.effect_size: A one-SD increase in media pessimism predicts an 8.1bp same-day decline in Dow Jones returns, with a 6.8bp reversal over the following 2-5 trading days (significant at 5%), i.e. roughly 85% of the initial move reverses within the week. Extreme pessimism also forecasts abnormally high trading volume.
findings.horizon: Same-day impact, reversing within ~1 trading week
findings.paper: Giving Content to Investor Sentiment: The Role of Media in the Stock Market
findings.caveats: Opened the full PDF directly (uts.edu.au mirror) and extracted text via pdftotext this session -- effect sizes above are read straight from the paper. Sample = WSJ 'Abreast of the Market' column, 1984-1999, and the measure is AGGREGATE stock-market (Dow Jones) sentiment, not firm-specific news. Old, heavily cited (7,500+ citations) result on a very short (days) horizon, so it says nothing directly about multi-year 'bumper' identification.
findings.applies_to_pre_profit_small_caps: Low direct transfer -- it is a market-wide, days-horizon sentiment/noise-trading result, not a single-name or multi-year signal. Its relevance here is indirect: it establishes that news-sentiment text analysis (NLP on press coverage) is a real, measurable, tradeable channel, which motivates building a firm-level news-sentiment feed for candidate bumpers rather than treating this paper's own numbers as applicable to small caps.

findings.signal: Attention-grabbing events (news coverage, abnormal trading volume, extreme one-day returns) driving retail buying pressure
findings.effect_size: Abstract only (numeric spread not captured this session): individual investors are net buyers, not sellers, of attention-grabbing stocks, because search costs constrain what they can buy but not what they already own and can sell. No dollar/bp effect size was retrieved from the primary text.
findings.horizon: Not specified in the material retrieved
findings.paper: All That Glitters: The Effect of Attention and News on the Buying Behavior of Individual and Institutional Investors
findings.caveats: Verified via Crossref abstract + RePEc/IDEAS citation page this session (1,520 citations recorded on RePEc). Could not reach a working full-text mirror (Berkeley faculty PDF returned 404, ResearchGate 403) to pull the quantitative buy-sell imbalance/return numbers, so only the mechanism, not the magnitude, is verified. The paper describes a BEHAVIORAL MECHANISM (why retail buys what it notices), not itself a proven positive-alpha strategy -- downstream literature (including the Robinhood paper below) shows that chasing attention this way tends to produce NEGATIVE subsequent returns.
findings.applies_to_pre_profit_small_caps: High conceptual relevance: pre-profit small/microcaps with no analyst coverage are discovered almost entirely via attention triggers (a press release, a volume spike, a viral post) rather than fundamentals research, so this mechanism is arguably stronger for exactly this population. But the mechanism describes retail buying pressure, not fundamental success probability -- it explains why a bumper gets bid up on hype, not whether the hype is justified.

findings.signal: Robinhood retail 'popularity'/mass-buying data as a real-time attention proxy
findings.effect_size: Average 20-trading-day abnormal returns of -4.7% for the stocks that were the top purchases by Robinhood users each day.
findings.horizon: 20 trading days (~1 month)
findings.paper: Attention-Induced Trading and Returns: Evidence from Robinhood Users
findings.caveats: Verified from the actual abstract text via Crossref this session. Sample is Robinhood users specifically (skews younger, less experienced, smaller account sizes) over roughly 2018-2020; the effect may partly reflect the platform's own feature design (e.g. simplified UI, gamification) rather than a universal 'reddit/retail attention' effect, per the authors' own hedge.
findings.applies_to_pre_profit_small_caps: Directly relevant and CAUTIONARY for the user's Nebius/IonQ/Quantum-bumper thesis: this is the closest match in the literature to 'robinhood/reddit attention chasing,' and the finding is that intense retail-attention buying FORECASTS NEGATIVE, not positive, 1-month abnormal returns. That argues attention alone (unconfirmed by other signals) is closer to a crowding/fade risk marker than a bumper-detection signal -- it flags where retail already is, which is late information for the retail crowd itself, though it says less about whether informed/institutional money has arrived first.

findings.signal: Customer-supplier economic links: lagged cross-predictability of linked-firm returns
findings.effect_size: A trading strategy long high-momentum customers' suppliers / short low-momentum customers' suppliers (built off economic-link data) 'yields monthly alphas of over 150 basis points.'
findings.horizon: Monthly rebalanced
findings.paper: Economic Links and Predictable Returns
findings.caveats: Abstract verified directly via the RePEc/IDEAS citation page this session, including the specific '150+ bps monthly alpha' figure. This is now an 18-year-old, extremely well-known result (part of the standard cross-sectional anomaly literature); per McLean & Pontiff (2016) below, published anomalies decay by roughly 50% on average post-publication, and customer-supplier links identified via 10-K disclosures are now systematically scraped by many quant shops, so the tradeable edge today is very likely smaller than the original 150bps.
findings.applies_to_pre_profit_small_caps: Very high -- this is the single most directly actionable mechanism for this repo, because it maps exactly onto the capital-web (supplier/customer graph) infrastructure already built here (CLAUDE.md capital-web-edge-semantics memory). The original sample, however, is disclosure-based customer-supplier pairs among CRSP/Compustat-covered firms with real revenue -- pre-revenue or newly-public small caps may not yet have the disclosed customer relationships (10-K 'major customer' footnotes) that identify the link in the first place, so the method needs adaptation (e.g. contract announcements, partnership press releases) rather than a direct lift for the pre-revenue case.

findings.signal: Supplier/customer industry segmentation and cross-predictability, moderated by analyst coverage and institutional ownership
findings.effect_size: Documents that (i) economically related supplier/customer-industry stocks cross-predict each other's returns, and (ii) the magnitude of that cross-predictability DECLINES with the level of analyst coverage and institutional ownership. No specific bp/alpha number was retrieved from the abstract text obtained this session.
findings.horizon: Not specified in the retrieved abstract (standard practice in this literature is monthly)
findings.paper: Market Segmentation and Cross-predictability of Returns
findings.caveats: Abstract verified directly via the Crossref API (full JATS abstract text retrieved) this session. Could not reach a working full-text mirror for the exact effect-size numbers (Chicago Booth faculty PDF link 404'd), so only the qualitative result, not a quantified spread, is confirmed.
findings.applies_to_pre_profit_small_caps: The single most useful qualitative finding in this set for a small/pre-profit-cap screen: the paper explicitly finds cross-predictability is STRONGER precisely where analyst coverage and institutional ownership are LOW -- i.e. in the under-covered, illiquid names that define the 'bumper' universe. This gives a concrete, testable hypothesis for the capital-web graph: watch price/news action in a well-covered, profitable downstream customer or upstream enabler, and look for a lag before it is reflected in an obscure, thinly-covered supplier's price.

findings.signal: Publication/discovery decay of academic return-predictor characteristics
findings.effect_size: Average out-of-sample decay in return predictability (statistical-bias explanation) is ~15%, not statistically distinguishable from zero. Average post-publication decay (statistical bias + price pressure from informed traders reacting to the paper) is ~50%, statistically different from both 0% and 100%.
findings.horizon: N/A -- meta-study across 56 published cross-sectional predictors
findings.paper: Does Academic Research Destroy Stock Return Predictability?
findings.caveats: Abstract verified directly via Crossref this session, including the specific 15%/50% figures.
findings.applies_to_pre_profit_small_caps: Applies as a discount factor to EVERY signal above once it is more than a few years old and has been publicly written up (as all of these have been, some 15-20+ years ago): expect roughly half the originally documented edge to have eroded from crowding, with the rest plausibly further eroded by transaction costs and small-cap illiquidity, which the McLean-Pontiff sample (large, liquid, CRSP/Compustat names) does not fully capture.

findings.signal: Aggregate job-openings-to-employment ratio (JOE) as a stock-market-wide return predictor
findings.effect_size: JOE 'outperforms a broad set of over two dozen popular predictor variables in both in-sample and out-of-sample forecasting tests' for the AGGREGATE equity premium; switching from a historical-mean forecast to a JOE-based forecast produces a 2.91% gain in annualized certainty-equivalent return and a 0.20 gain in annualized Sharpe ratio.
findings.horizon: Standard predictive-regression horizon (paper does not specify a single horizon in the retrieved abstract; likely monthly/annual as is standard in this literature)
findings.paper: Job Postings and Aggregate Stock Returns
findings.authors_year: (SSRN working paper 2018; published Journal of Financial Markets 64:100804, June 2023)
findings.caveats: Abstract verified via Crossref this session (SSRN working-paper version had a full abstract; the published Journal of Financial Markets record had no abstract in Crossref's metadata, only title/venue/page). IMPORTANT MISMATCH WITH THE TASK: this paper's 'job postings' signal is the MARKET-WIDE ratio of job openings to total employment (a macro/market-timing variable), not company-specific hiring data (e.g. an individual firm's LinkedIn/Indeed job-posting growth) that would flag a single bumper candidate is scaling up hiring. I ran targeted searches (Crossref bibliographic search) for a firm-level 'company job postings predict that company's stock return' academic paper and did not find one -- this appears to be a genuine gap in the peer-reviewed literature as distinct from industry/fintech data products (e.g. Revelio Labs, Thinknum) that sell firm-level hiring data to funds without a public peer-reviewed validation I could locate this session.
findings.applies_to_pre_profit_small_caps: Low direct transfer as found -- it is a market-timing signal, not a stock-picking one, so it would not distinguish one pre-profit small cap from another. The user's actual instinct (watch a specific company's hiring, e.g. R&D headcount ramp at a quantum-computing startup) is NOT the thing this paper studies; flag this as an assumption/untested idea rather than literature-backed until a firm-level study is found.

findings.signal: SPAC / de-SPAC mergers as a 'pre-profit disruptive-sector' vehicle
findings.effect_size: de-SPAC investors experience 'steep post-merger losses' -- net cash per share actually delivered to the merged company was a median $4.10-$5.70 versus the $10.00/share raised in the SPAC IPO (Jan 2019-June 2020 primary sample). Separately, Ritter's updated long-run return table (directly opened PDF this session, Table 15c, sourced from Gahng, Ritter & Zhang, Review of Financial Studies, Sept 2023) shows average market-adjusted 3-year buy-and-hold deSPAC returns ranging roughly from about -60% to -135% across 2012-2017 merger-year cohorts (small early-cohort sample sizes, 1-13 deals/year) -- i.e. deeply negative vs. the matched market in every cohort reported.
findings.horizon: 1-year and 3-year post-merger buy-and-hold
findings.paper: A Sober Look at SPACs (structural/cost analysis); SPACs (post-merger long-run returns, as tabulated in Ritter's 'Initial Public Offerings: Updated Long-run Statistics')
findings.authors_year: Klausner, Ohlrogge & Ruan (2022); Gahng, Ritter & Zhang (2023)
findings.url_or_doi: SSRN 10.2139/ssrn.3720919 (Klausner et al.); Review of Financial Studies Sept 2023 (Gahng, Ritter & Zhang), figures as reproduced in Ritter's live table at https://site.warrington.ufl.edu/ritter/files/IPOs-long-run-returns-on-IPOs.pdf
findings.caveats: Klausner/Ohlrogge/Ruan abstract verified via Crossref this session. The Ritter table was directly downloaded and parsed (pdftotext) this session from the live, continuously-updated University of Florida page (last table update noted as 'updated on July 29, 2026' inside the document) -- note this is a BASE-RATE/DESCRIPTIVE table, not itself a peer-reviewed inferential paper, though it is the standard reference dataset the academic IPO/SPAC literature cites. The de-SPAC 3-year figures for 2018-2024 cohorts were present in the source table but blank/incomplete in the text-extraction (insufficient elapsed time for a full 3-year window as of the 2026 update), so only 2012-2017 cohorts have complete 3-year figures.
findings.applies_to_pre_profit_small_caps: Directly on point -- SPACs were the vehicle of choice in 2020-2021 for exactly the 'not-yet-profitable, high-narrative-upside' companies (EV, space, quantum-adjacent, etc.) the user is describing, and the base rate is that this vehicle specifically has delivered systematically poor, not just volatile, investor outcomes on average, independent of whether the underlying sector thesis (e.g. EVs) was directionally right.

base_rates: Ritter (University of Florida, IPO long-run-return database; PDF directly opened and parsed this session, table dated 2026): across 9,195 U.S. operating-company IPOs from 1975-2021, the MEAN 3-year buy-and-hold return (from first closing price) is +21.2%, but the MEDIAN is -25.7% -- i.e. the typical/median IPO loses about a quarter of its value over 3 years and the positive mean is driven by a small number of large winners (classic right-skew/lottery distribution). Over 5 years the mean is +37.8% but the median is -32.0%. Restricting to larger IPOs (LTM sales >= $100M, a rough proxy for less speculative issuers) improves the median to roughly +2.6% (3-yr) and -1.2% (5-yr) -- still close to a coin flip, not a reliable edge.

Ritter Table 16b (same source, directly opened): firms that were UNPROFITABLE at IPO (n=3,926, 1980-2024) had an average 3-year market-adjusted buy-and-hold return of -30.7% (style-adjusted -23.4%), versus PROFITABLE-at-IPO firms (n=5,327) at -13.0% market-adjusted (style-adjusted +1.8%). This is the most directly relevant base rate to the user's question: on average, pre-profit newly-public companies underperform the market by roughly 20-30 percentage points over 3 years as a GROUP, even though (per the median/mean gap above) a small subset of that same group produces the outsized 'bumper' winners the user wants to find early.

Ritter Table 16c (directly opened): TECH-sector IPOs specifically (n=2,689, 1980-2023 excluding the 1999-2000 bubble) beat the average: mean 3-year style-adjusted return +46.0% vs. -1.6% for non-tech, and market-adjusted +25.8% vs. -14.7% for non-tech -- i.e. sector selection (tech/growth) has historically mattered a great deal, consistent with the user's instinct to focus on an emerging-sector bet, though this is a mean (skew-driven), not a median/hit-rate, figure.

de-SPAC mergers (Klausner/Ohlrogge/Ruan 2022; Gahng/Ritter/Zhang 2023, via Ritter's updated table, directly opened this session): median net cash actually delivered to the merged company was $4.10-$5.70 per $10.00 raised, and average market-adjusted 3-year post-merger returns were deeply negative (roughly -60% to -135%) in every merger-year cohort with complete data (2012-2017) -- the SPAC wrapper specifically, as distinct from the underlying sector thesis, has a poor historical base rate.

McLean & Pontiff (2016, Journal of Finance, abstract verified via Crossref this session): across 56 published academic return-predictor characteristics, average post-publication decay in predictive power is about 50% (statistically distinct from both 0% and 100%); apply this as a rough discount to every 'edge' number cited above once the signal has been public for years, as all of the attention/economic-link papers here have been.

Not independently verified this session (flagging explicitly rather than asserting): the widely-cited Bessembinder (2018, Journal of Financial Economics 129:440-457, 'Do Stocks Outperform Treasury Bills?') finding that a small minority of all listed U.S. common stocks (commonly cited as roughly the top 4%) account for essentially all of the stock market's lifetime wealth creation above Treasury bills, with the majority of individual stocks underperforming T-bills over their listed life. I confirmed the citation (journal, volume, pages) via Crossref but could not reach an open copy of the actual text this session (SSRN blocked by bot-detection, faculty mirrors 404'd), so treat the specific percentage as inferred/recalled rather than verified-this-session; it is directionally consistent with, and reinforces, the median-vs-mean IPO skew documented directly above from Ritter's data.

No canonical peer-reviewed academic study was found (Crossref bibliographic search, this session) directly testing 'government contract award announcements predict abnormal returns in small/micro-cap contractors' or 'firm-level job-posting growth predicts that firm's stock returns.' Both appear in commercial alt-data/practitioner use (e.g. USASpending.gov contract feeds, Revelio Labs/Thinknum hiring data) but I could not locate a peer-reviewed academic validation of either as a firm-specific signal -- flagging this as an open literature gap rather than filling it with an unverified claim.

kept.reason: Empirical study shows near-null separation in the target population: AUC(rev_growth_yoy)=0.51 and AUC(rev_acceleration)=0.48 in tech_small (n~30-80/arm) — acceleration is actually LOWER in winners than matched controls in that subgroup, and even the "all" sample AUCs (0.55/0.51) are weak versus shares_growth_yoy (0.61) or the strong below-0.5 cluster (margin/OCF/momentum/drawdown), which is where the study's real signal lives. Several of the best winner case-study instances are self-labeled coincident/trigger events (NVDA and VRT explicitly "confirming, not leading"; PLTR instances at 2 months) rather than genuine advance warnings, so the family's lead time is inconsistent — real (4-22mo) in a minority of instances, ~0mo in others. Survivorship risk is high: the graveyard cohort (NKLA/RIDE/GOEV/Lordstown/Canoo/Arrival/Hyliion) never reached a revenue-inflection stage (their failure modes were fake order books, governance capture, or disclosed runway), so there is no failed-name counterexample to test the signal against — the winner list was built retrospectively from known successes. Data is genuinely free and scriptable at scale (SEC EDGAR XBRL revenue lines, 8-K Ex-99.1 releases; the study itself computed this across 636 names with ~45% XBRL coverage), and it is knowable within a filing-lag window (days for 8-K, quarters for 10-Q/10-K), so it's not unknowable in time — just weak and inconsistently leading. Literature supplied is silent on this specific factor (covers R&D/patents/org-capital instead), with the one relevant meta-finding (McLean & Pontiff) warning that anomaly returns of this modest size decay heavily out-of-sample. Net: not contradicted enough to refute outright, but far too weak (near-coin-flip AUC in the pre-profit small-cap population that matters most) and too survivorship-tainted to serve as a primary discriminator.

(1) Survivorship: the raw signal is contaminated. The graveyard discriminators for this exact case type explicitly show collapsed names carrying the identical surface signal — RIDE's 100,000 "pre-orders," GOEV's Walmart/Kingbee/Zeeba deals (fewer than 12 vehicles ever delivered), GM's Nikola equity stake, Foxconn's Lordstown commitment, Arrival's UPS LOI with zero deposit/cancellation penalty. These read as "anchor customer/contract" announcements indistinguishable on the press release from NVDA's cloud-provider wins or CRWV's Microsoft concentration. The discriminator the graveyard data itself names is not "is there a named customer" but whether the deal is binding (deposit, no easy-out termination clause) and whether subsequent 10-Qs show actual delivered units/recognized revenue/growing RPO — a verification layer, not the presence of the announcement. So the family as stated (binary anchor-customer flag) does not cleanly separate winners from failures; a refined version (binding + confirmed-in-arrears) would, but that requires reading filing language, not a scriptable numeric field. (2) Look-ahead: knowable in time with real, checkable lag — instances here run 5-18 months before the run (NVDA 8-K CFO commentary 18mo, VRT 10-K 6mo, PLTR contract award 15mo, CRWV S-1 RPO 6mo), all via disclosures that predate the price move. No look-ahead problem. (3) Free data: yes — SEC EDGAR full-text search and XBRL customer-concentration risk-factor tags, 8-K/press-release contract announcements, USAspending.gov contract awards, company IR — all free and in principle scriptable across ~500 names, though the binding-vs-hollow check the graveyard data says actually matters requires reading filing text (deposit/termination-clause language), not a clean numeric lookup, so full automation at scale is partial. (4) Literature/empirical study: neither addresses this family directly. The cited literature (R&D intensity, patents, organization capital, MAX effect) has no customer-concentration/anchor-contract factor, and today's 336-winner empirical study computed no AUC for this feature at all — it is simply untested by the quantitative evidence supplied, so there is no numeric confirmation either way, only the qualitative case-study pattern (present in essentially every listed winner) weighed against the graveyard's warning that the same pattern shows up in busts. Net: not refuted (no evidence it points the wrong way), but the demonstrated failure mode in structurally identical past cases and the absence of a validating backtest keep it out of "core." Use it as a supporting screen — flag names with newly-disclosed hyperscaler/named-customer relationships or contract wins as candidates — but require the graveyard's verification layer (binding terms, subsequent-quarter delivery/revenue confirmation, RPO/backlog trend) before treating it as a standalone go/no-go signal.

The 14 case-study instances (AMD Zen, ENPH IQ7, TSLA Shanghai, SMCI Taiwan plant, VRT backlog, NBIS/IREN/APLD/CRWV GPU fleets, QBTS Advantage2, ASTS satellite capex roadmap, RKLB cadence, PLTR bootcamps) are all knowable well before the run (6-22 months lead, median ~10-13) from free sources — SEC EDGAR 10-K/10-Q/8-K/6-K/S-1 (Item 2 Properties, MD&A capex tables, XBRL PaymentsToAcquirePropertyPlantAndEquipment tag), company IR press releases, and trade press. Scaling to ~500 names is a straightforward EDGAR full-text-search + XBRL frames pull, so free_data_exists and observable_in_time are both true with high confidence (verified against the URLs/evidence given in the task, not independently re-fetched this session per the no-search constraint).

Survivorship is the problem. The graveyard discriminators supplied here are explicit that the thing separating collapses (NKLA, RIDE, GOEV, Lordstown, Canoo, Arrival) from survivors was never the presence of an 'order,' 'capacity,' or 'plant' announcement — it was whether the DEMAND behind that capacity was binding (deposits, non-cancellable contracts, delivered units), whether governance/related-party structure was clean, and whether disclosed cash runway could fund the buildout. Several of those specific collapsed names (Lordstown's actual Ohio assembly plant acquired from GM, Canoo's Oklahoma manufacturing deal, Arrival's microfactories) are themselves capex/capacity announcements that would score identically to SMCI's Taiwan plant or NBIS's GPU clusters on a bare 'capacity disclosed ahead of revenue' feature (this specific point about Lordstown/Canoo/Arrival's own capacity announcements is inferred from well-known public record, not re-verified via a fetched source this session — flagging per epistemic-honesty rule). So the raw family is present in both cohorts and cannot discriminate alone; it needs to be conditioned on the graveyard's binding-demand/runway/governance overlay to have any signal value. That is a structural, not incidental, confound — hence high survivorship risk.
